sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. HamolN (S, Mgh, Msb, K, &c., in some copies of the S HimolN ) and HumolaAnN , (Mgh, K,) He bore it, carried it, took it up and carried it, conveyed it, or carried it off or away, (MA,) EalaY Zahorihi (S, MA,) upon his back, or EalaY raA^osihi upon his head; (MA;) and ↓ AHtmlhu signifies the same: (Msb, K:) or the latter is used in relation to an object inconsiderable and small in comparison with that in relation to which the former is used; as in the saying of En-Nábighah, (TA,) A_in~aA A@qotasamonaA xuT~atayonaA bayonanaA fajaAri ↓ faHamalota bar~apa waA@Hotamalotu [ Verily we have divided our two qualities between us, and thou hast borne as thy share goodness, and I have borne as my share wickedness ]. (TA * in the present art., and S and TA &c. in arts. br and fjr .) Hence, in the Kur [xx. 100], faA_in~ahu yaHomilu yawoma AlqiyaAmapi wizorFA [ He shall bear, on the day of resurrection, a heavy burden ]. (TA.) Hence also, in the Kur [vii. 189], Hamalato HamolFA xafiyfFA [ She bore a light burden ]; (S, TA;) i. e., [as some say,] the seminal fluid. (TA.) Hence also, in the Kur [xxix. 60], wakaA^ay~ino mino daAb~apK laA taHomilu rizoqahaA [ And how many a beast is there that does not bear its sustenance ! ], meaning, (assumed tropical:) does not provide its sustenance, but is sustained by God. (TA.) yaHomilu AlHaTaba [lit. He carries firewood ], (A in art. HTb ,) or AlHaTaba Alr~aToba [ juicy, or fresh, firewood ], (Er-Rághib, TA,) means (tropical:) he goes about with calumny, or slander. (A in art. HTb , and Er-Rághib * and TA. *) ― -b2- Hamalahu EalaY Ald~aAb~ap , (Msb, TA,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. HamolN , (Msb, TA,) [ He carried him, or mounted him, (namely, a man, Msb) upon the beast; as also ↓ AHtmlhu .] And Hamalahu [alone] He gave him a beast upon which to ride. (T, TA. [See Kur ix. 93.]) A^aHomalahu is not used in this sense. (T, TA.) ― -b3- See also 4. ― -b4- Hamalati AlmaroA^apu , aor. , (K,) inf. n. HamolN , (TA,) (tropical:) The woman became pregnant, or conceived: (K, TA:) and Hamalato waladahaA She became pregnant with, or conceived, her child: (Msb:) one should not say, Hamalato bihi ; or this is rare; (K;) or one should not say this, but it is frequently said; (IJ, TA;) [for] as Hamalato is syn. with Ealiqato , (Msb, TA,) and the latter is trans. by means of bi the former is thus made trans., (TA,) therefore one says, Hamalato bihi fiY layolapi ka*aA wafiY mawoDiEi ka*aA , meaning She became pregnant with him, or conceived him, in such a night, and in such a place. (Msb.) Hamalato is also said of a ewe or she-goat, and of a female beast of prey, [and app. of any female,] accord. to IAar; meaning (assumed tropical:) She was, or became, in the first stage of pregnancy. (TA.) ― -b5- Hamalati Al$~ajarapu , inf. n. HamolN , (assumed tropical:) The tree [ bore, or] produced, or put forth, its fruit. (Msb.) ― -b6- Hamala bidayonK , and bidiyapK , inf. n. HamaAlapN , (assumed tropical:) [ He bore, or took upon himself, the responsibility, or he was, or became, responsible, for a debt, and a bloodwit: ] (Msb:) [for] Hamala bihi , aor. , inf. n. HamaAlapN , signifies kafala . (S, * K.) And Hamala AlHamaAlapa and ↓ tHm~lhA (assumed tropical:) [ He was, or became, responsible for the bloodwit, or debt or the like ]: both signify the same: (S, TA:) and bihi ↓ tHm~l (assumed tropical:) He took it upon himself, or became responsible, or answerable, for it: (Msb in art. kfl :) and muEoZamahu ↓ tHm~l (assumed tropical:) He took, or imposed, upon himself, or undertook, the main part of it: (Jel in xxiv. 11:) and AlA^amora ↓ AHtml (assumed tropical:) He took, or imposed, upon himself, or undertook, the thing, or affair; he bore, or took upon himself, the burden thereof. (L in art. qld .) You say, Hamala qawomN Eano qawomK diyapF , (K, TA,) or garaAmapF , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) [ A party bore, or took upon itself, for a party, the responsibility for a bloodwit, or a debt or the like; ] as also ↓ tHm~l . (S.) [And Hamala Eano fulaAnK lifulaAnK ka*aA (assumed tropical:) He bore, or took upon himself, for such a one, the responsibility, to such a one, for such a thing. ] And HamaAlapF bayona ↓ tHm~l qawomK (assumed tropical:) He bore, or took upon himself, the responsibility for the bloodwits between people, in order to make peace between them, when war had occurred between them, and men's blood had been shed. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b7- Hamala ZulomFA (assumed tropical:) [ He made himself chargeable with wrongdoing ]. (Kur xx. 110.) ― -b8- [ Hamala AlA^amaAnapa : see A^amaAnapN : accord. to some, it means (assumed tropical:) He took upon himself, or accepted, the trust: accord. to others, he was unfaithful to it: and ↓ AiHotamalahaA means the same.] ― -b9- Hamalotu A_idolaAlahu : see 8. ― -b10- Hamala Eanohu : see 8. ― -b11- Hamala fulaAnN AlHiqoda EalaY fulaAnK (assumed tropical:) Such a one [ bore or] concealed in his mind rancour, malevolence, malice, or spite, against such a one. (TA.) And fulaAnN laA yaHomilu , i. e. yuZohiru gaDabahu [which may be meant as the explanation of lA yHml , i. e. (assumed tropical:) Such a one shows (or will not conceal ) his anger; and thus SM understood it; or as the explanation of yHml alone, i. e. such a one will not show his anger ]: (Az, TA:) [for] Hamala AlgaDaba , (K,) aor. , inf. n. HamolN , (TA,) means (tropical:) he showed, or manifested, anger. (K, TA.) And hence, it is said, is the saying, in a trad., A_i*aA balaga AlmaA='u qul~atayoni lamo yaHomilo xabavFA , i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ When the water amounts to the quantity of two vessels of the kind called qul~ap ,] impurity does not appear in it: (O, K, * TA:) or the meaning is, (assumed tropical:) it does not admit the bearing of impurity: for one says, fulaAnN laA yaHomilu AlD~ayoma , i. e. (assumed tropical:) such a one refuses to bear, or submit to, and repels from himself, injury. (Msb.) You say also, Hamala mino *`lika A^anafFA (assumed tropical:) He conceived, in consequence of that, disdain, or scorn, arising from indignation and anger. (TA in art. Anf , from a trad.) ― -b12- Hamala AlHadiyva (assumed tropical:) [ He bore in his memory, knowing by heart, the tradition, or narrative, or story; and in like manner, AlquroA=na the Kur-án ]. (Msb in art. rwY .) ― -b13- Hamala fulaAnFA , and bihi ↓ tHm~l and Ealayohi , (assumed tropical:) He relied upon such a one in intercession, and in a case of need. (TA.) ― -b14- Humila EalaY Aln~aAqapi (assumed tropical:) The she-camel was covered by a stallion. (M in art. Smd .) ― -b15- Hamala Ealyohi [as syn. with Ham~alahu ]: see 2, in three places. ― -b16- Hamala EalaY daAb~atihi fawoqa TaAqatihaA fiY Als~ayori (assumed tropical:) [ He tasked his beast beyond its power in journeying, or marching, or in respect of pace ]. (S in art. jhd .) And Hamala EalaY nafosihi fiY Als~ayori (assumed tropical:) He jaded, or fatigued, himself, or tasked himself beyond his power, in journeying, or marching. (S, TA.) [See also 6.] ― -b17- Hamala Ealayohi fiY AlHarobi , inf. n. HamolapN [which is properly an inf. n. of un.], (T, S,) (assumed tropical:) He charged, or made an assault or attack, upon him in war, or battle. (TA.) ― -b18- Hamalotu EalaY baniY fulaAnK (assumed tropical:) I made mischief, or I excited disorder, disagreement, dissension, or strife, between, or among, the sons of such a one. (AZ, S.) ― -b19- Hamalahu EalaY AlA^amori , aor. , (assumed tropical:) He incited, excited, urged, instigated, induced, or made, him to do the thing, or affair. (ISd, K.) ― -b20- [ Hamala lafoZFA EalaY lafoZK A=xara , aor. , inf. n. HamolN , a phrase often used in lexicology and grammar, (assumed tropical:) He made, or held, a word, or an expression, to accord in form, or in meaning, or syntactically, with another word, or expression. One says, yuHomalu EalaY AlA^akovari (assumed tropical:) It (a word) is made to accord in form with those words with which it may be compared that constitute the greater number: thus one says of raHomaAnu , which is made to accord in form with words of the measure faEolaAnu , though it has not a fem. of the measure faEolaY , in preference to faEolaAnN , because words of the measure faEolaAnu are more numerous than those of the measure faEolaAnN . And yuHomalu EalaY naqiyDihi (assumed tropical:) It (a word) is made to accord in form with its contrary in meaning: thus EijaAfN , an anomalous pl. of A^aEoHafu , is made to accord. in form with simaAnN , a regular pl. of samiynN . And yaHmalu EalaY AlmaEonaY (assumed tropical:) It (a word) is made to accord syntactically with its meaning: and yuHomalu EalaY All~afoZi (assumed tropical:) It is made to accord syntactically with its grammatical character: the former is said when, in a sentence, we make a mase. word fem., and the contrary, because the meaning allows us to substitute a fem. syn. for the masc. word, and a masc. syn. for the fem. word: for ex., it is said in the Kur vi. 78, falam~aA raA^aY Al$~amosa baAzigapF qaAla h`*aA rab~iY “ And when he saw the sun rising, he said, This is my Lord: ” here (by saying bAzgp ) Al$ms is first made to accord syntactically with its grammatical character ( tuHomalu EalaY All~afoZi ); and then (by saying h`*aA instead of h`*ihi ) it is made to accord syntactically with its meaning ( tuHomalu EalaY AlmaEonaY ), which is Aljirom or the like: this is allowable; but the reverse in respect of order is of weak authority; because the meaning is of more importance than the grammatical character of the word. (Collected from the Kull pp. 156 and 157, and other works.)] ― -b21- Hamalahu A^aHosana maHoyalK (assumed tropical:) [ He put the best construction upon it; namely, a saying: mHml being here an inf. n.]. (TA in art. Abw ) ― -b22- [ Hamalahu EalaY Aln~aAsixi (assumed tropical:) He attributed it to, or charged it upon, the copyist; namely, a mistake. Humila ElaY Aln~aAsixi , said of a mistake, occurs in the K in art. rbx ― -b23- EalaY A=xara Hamala $ayoy^FA , in logic, means (assumed tropical:) He predicated a thing of another thing.] ― -b24- See also HumolaAnN .

definition: [ He bore, bore his weight, pressed, or pressed heavily, upon it, or him ].
sourceDefinition: [ He bore, bore his weight, pressed, or pressed heavily, upon it, or him ]. You say, taHaAmala EalaY raA^osi rumoHihi muEotamidFA Ealayohi liyamuwta [ He bore, bore his weight, pressed, or pressed heavily, upon the head of his spear, leaning upon it, in order that he might die ]. (Mgh in art. rkz .) And taHaAmalotu Ealayohi kaAlEaASiri [ I pressed, or pressed heavily, upon it, like the squeezer of fruit &c.]. (Msb in art. hmz .) ― -b2- [Hence,] (assumed tropical:) He wronged him; or treated him wrongfully, or unjustly. (S, Mgh, and Har p. 80.) And it is asserted that one says, tHAml Alz~amaAnu Eano fulaAnK meaning (assumed tropical:) Time, or fortune, turned from such a one, and took away his property: and tHAml A_ilayohi (assumed tropical:) It became favourable to him. (Har ibid.) ― -b3- [Also] (assumed tropical:) He imposed upon him, or tasked him with, that which he was not able to bear, or to do. (M, O, K.) And tHAml EalaY nafosihi , (S, O,) or tHAml fiY AlA^amori and biAlA^amori , (M, K,) (assumed tropical:) He imposed upon himself, or tasked himself with, or constrained himself to do, the thing, or affair, notwithstanding difficulty, or trouble, or inconvenience, (S, M, O, K,) and fatigue. (M, TA.) And taHaAmalotu fiY Alma$oYi (assumed tropical:) I constrained myself to walk, notwithstanding difficulty, or trouble, or inconvenience, and fatigue: whence, rub~amaA yataHaAmalu AlS~ayodu wayaTiyru , i. e. (assumed tropical:) Sometimes the game will constrain itself to fly, notwithstanding difficulty, &c., and will fly. (Mgh.) [See also two similar phrases in the first paragraph.] ― -b4- ↓ mutaHaAmalN is used as its inf. n., and also as a noun of place: using it as an inf. n., you say, maAfiY fulaAnK mutaHaAmalN i. e. taHaAmulN (assumed tropical:) [ There is not, in such a one, wrongdoing, &c.]: and using it of a place, h`*aA mutaHaAmalunaA (assumed tropical:) [ This is our place of wrong-doing, or wrongtreatment, &c.]. (S, TA.)

sourceDefinition: A lamb; i. e. the young one of the ewe in the first year; (Mgh, Msb;) i. q. baraqN ; (S;) or xaruwfN [explained in the K in art. xrf as the male young one of the sheep-kind; or such as has pastured, and become strong ]: (K, and S and Msb in art. xrf :) or such as is termed ja*aEN , [i. e. a year old, or from six to ten months, ] of the young of the sheep-kind; and less than this [ in age ]: (ISd, K:) accord. to Er-Rághib, it signifies maHomuwlN [ borne, or carried ]; and the young of the sheep-kind is particularly called thus because borne, or carried, on account of its impotence, and of the nearness of the time when its mother was pregnant with it: (TA:) pl. HumolaAnN (S, M, Mgh, Sgh, Msb, K) and A^aHomaAlN . (M, K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] AlHamalu (assumed tropical:) [ The sign Aries; ] a certain sign of the zodiac; (K;) the first of the signs of the zodiac; (S;) the constellation comprising, first, the $araTaAni , which are its two horns; then, the buTayon ; then, the vuray~aA . (T, TA.) One says, muTironaA binawo'i AlHamali and bnw' AlT~aliY~i (assumed tropical:) [ We were, or have been, given rain by the auroral setting of Aries: so the pagan Arabs used to say: see nawo'N ; and see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl ]. (TA.) One says also, h`*aA HamalN TaAliEFA (assumed tropical:) [ This is Aries, rising ]; suppressing the Al , but making the noun to remain determinate; and thus one does in the case of every name of a sign of the zodiac, preserving the Al or suppressing it. (TA.) ― -b3- HamalN signifies also (tropical:) Clouds containing much water: (M, K, TA:) or black clouds: (T, TA: [see also HawomalN , below:]) or, as some say, the rain [ supposed to be given ] by the nawo' [see above] of AlHamal . (TA.)

definition: [ Bearing, carrying, taking up and carrying, conveying, or carrying off or away;
sourceDefinition: [ Bearing, carrying, taking up and carrying, conveying, or carrying off or away; ] act. part. n. of 1 having for its object what is borne on the back [&c.]: (Msb:) fem. with p : (S, Msb:) pl. masc. HamalapN : (S, TA:) and pl. fem. HaAmilaAtN . (TA.) Hence, Hamalapu AlEaro$i [ The bearers of the Er$ , or empyrean, held by the vulgar to be the throne of God ]. (S, TA.) And the phrase faA@loHaAmilaAti wiqorFA [in the Kur li. 2, lit. And the bearers of a load, or heavy load: ] meaning (assumed tropical:) the clouds. (TA.) ― -b2- Applied to a woman, (tropical:) Pregnant; (S, Mgh, Msb, K, &c.;) as also HaAmilapN : (S, Msb, K:) the former as being an epithet exclusively applied to a female: the latter as conformable to its verb, which is Hamalato ; (S, Msb;) or as being used in a tropical [or doubly tropical] manner, meaning pregnant in past time or in future time; (Msb;) or as a possessive epithet [meaning having a burden in the womb ]: (TA:) [see an ex. of the latter in a verse cited in the first paragraph of art. mxS :] accord. to the Koofees, the former, not being applied to a male, has no need of the sign of the fem. gender: but the Basrees say that this [rule] does not uniformly obtain; for the Arabs say rajulN A^ay~imN and AimoraA^apN A^ay~imN , and rajulN EaAnisN and AimoraA^apN EaAnisN ; and that, correctly speaking, HaAmilN and TaAliqN and HaAy^iDN and the like are epithets masc. in form applied to females, like as raboEapN and raAwiyapN and xujaA^apN are epithets fem. in form applied to males. (S.) It is also applied to a she-camel [and app. to any female] in the same sense. (Mgh.) ― -b3- Applied to trees ( $ajarN ), (assumed tropical:) Bearing fruit: (TA:) fem. with p . (K.) ― -b4- See also HamiylN . ― -b5- [Respecting this epithet, and the phrases HaAmilu AlA^amaAnapi and muHotamilu AlA^amaAnapi , see also A^amaAnapN , last sentence but one.] ― -b6- Hamalapu AlquraA=ni (assumed tropical:) [ Those who bear in their memory the Kur-án, knowing it by heart ]. (S, TA.)

sourceDefinition: [of which the primary signification is A place of bearing or carrying ], (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) or ↓ miHomalN [which primarily signifies An instrument for bearing or carrying ], (M, Mgh,) or the latter is allowable, (Msb,) The [ kind of vehicle called ] hawodaj ; (Msb;) as also ↓ HimolN : (M, K:) or the large hwdj termed Haj~aAjiY~N : (Mgh:) or a pair of dorsers, or panniers, or oblong chests, ( $iq~aAni ,) upon a camel, in which are borne two equal loads, (K,) [ and which, with a small tent over them, compose a hwdj ;] first made use of by El-Hajjáj Ibn-Yoosuf Eth-Thakafee: (TA:) one of the maHaAmil of the pilgrims: (S:) maHaAmilu being the pl. [What is now particularly termed the mHml (vulgarly pronounced maHomal ) of the pilgrims is an ornamented hwdj , which is borne by a camel, but without a rider, and is regarded as the royal banner of the caravan; such as is described and figured in my work on the Modern Egyptians. (See also maHaArapN , in art. Hwr .)] Its application to (tropical:) The camel that bears the mHml is tropical. (Mgh.) [See also HimolN . sourceDefinition: xAbrhu , (TA,) inf. n. maxaAbarapN , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K, &c.,) [ He made a contract, or bargain, with him to till and sow and cultivate land for a share of its produce: ] the inf. n. signifies i. q. muzaAraEapN [i. e. the making a contract, or bargain, with another to cultivate land for a share of its produce ], (AO, Lh, S, A, IAth, Mgh, Msb,) for somewhat of its produce, (S, Msb,) or for a third or a quarter, (AO, Mgh,) or for a determined share, such as a third or a quarter or some other portion, (IAth,) or for half or the like: (so in some copies of the K and in the TA:) or the tilling the ground for half or the like: (so in other copies of the K:) and i. q. muw^aAkarapN : (K:) and ↓ xiborN is syn. with muxaAbarapN : (S, K:) it is a forbidden practice: (A, Mgh, TA:) it is from xabiyrN signifying “ a tiller, or cultivator, of land: ” (S, Mgh:) or from xabara “ he furrowed, or ploughed (land) for sowing; ” whence xabiyrN also: (Msb:) or from xabirati AlA^aroDu “ the land abounded with xabaAr : ” or from [the fortress of] xayobar , because the Prophet made it to remain in the possession of its inhabitants for half of its revenue; and therefore it was said, xaAbarahumo . (TA.)

definition: [originally] an inf.

sourceDefinition: Knowing; having knowledge; (S, A, Msb;) as also ↓ xabirN : (AHn:) or possessing much knowledge with respect to internal things; like $ahiydN with respect to external things: (L in art. $hd :) or possessing knowledge of matters of information, news, tidings, accounts, narratives, or stories; of what is termed xabarN ; (K;) or of what are termed A^axobaAr ; (TA;) as also ↓ xaAbirN and ↓ xabirN , (K,) which last is thought by ISd to be a possessive [as distinguished from a verbal] epithet, (TA,) [or it is from xabira , a form which ISd may not have known,] and ↓ xuborN , (K,) which is an intensive epithet: (TA:) also informed; possessing information. (TA.) You say, A^anaA bihi xabiyrN I have knowledge of it. (A.) And [hence] Alxabiyru is a name of God, meaning He who knoweth what hath been and what is or will be: (TA:) or He who well knoweth the internal qualities of things. (Sharh Et-Tirmidhee.) ― -b2- Also Possessing knowledge of God, (K, TA,) by being acquainted with his names and his attributes. (TA.) ― -b3- A lawyer; one skilled in the law, or practical religion. (TA.) ― -b4- A head, or chief. (TA.) -A2- A tiller, or cultivator, of land. (S, Mgh, Msb, K.) -A3- Fur, or soft hair, syn. wabarN , (S, K,) of camels, and (tropical:) of the wild ass. [See also xabiyrapN below.] ― -b3- (tropical:) Plants, or herbage; (S, K, TA;) fresh herbage: (K, TA:) likened to the wabar of camels, because growing like the latter: and seed-produce. (TA.) It is said in a trad., nasotaxolibu Alxabiyra (tropical:) We cut (S, TA) with the reaping-hook, (TA,) and eat, the plants, or herbage. (S, TA.) ― -b4- Froth, or foam: (TA:) or the froth, or foam, of the mouths of camels. (S, K, TA.) -A4- Seasoned, or made savoury. (TA.) ― -b2- See also xuborapN .

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. xuDuwEN (S, Msb, K) and xaDoEN and xuDoEaAnN , or xiDoEaAnN , (TA,) He was, or became, lowly, humble, or submissive, (S, Msb, K,) lahu to him, (Msb, TA,) [for instance,] to his creditor, (Msb,) or to God; (TA;) as also ↓ AxtDE , (S, K,) [and ↓ AnxDE , (K in art. x*A^ ,)] and ↓ AixoDawoDaEa : (Sgh, K:) xuDuwEN is nearly the same as xu$uwEN , except that the latter is mostly used in relation to the voice [or the eyes]; but the former is used as meaning in the necks: (Msb:) or the former is in the body, ('Eyn and K in art. x$E ,) and signifies the acknowledgment of humility and submission; ('Eyn;) and the latter is in the voice and in the eyes. ('Eyn and K ubi suprà.) It is said in a trad. respecting the [devils'] hearing [the words of the angels] by stealth, xuDoEaAnFA liqawolihi [ With submissiveness to his saying, or to what he said ]; or, accord. to one relation, xiDoEaAnFA ; but it may be a pl. of xaADiEN ; and accord. to another relation, it is xuD~aEFA , which is a pl. of xaADiEN . (TA.) ― -b2- He was, or became, still, (K, TA,) and tractable, or submissive. (TA.) ― -b3- He made his words soft to a woman; as also ↓ AxDE : (L:) or the latter signifies his speech was soft to a woman. (O, K.) It is said in the Kur [xxxiii. 32], falaA taxoDaEona biAlqawoli Then be ye not soft in speech. (TA.) And you say, xaDaEa lahaA bikalaAmihi waxaDaEato lahu wataTam~aEa fiyhaA [ He was soft to her in speech, and she was soft to him, and he became excited to feel an eager desire for her, or to lust after her ]; (TA;) and in like manner, ↓ xaADaEahA , (K, * TA,) inf. n. muxaADaEapN , (TA,) [ he was soft in his speech to her, she being soft in her speech to him. ] And xaDaEaA bayonahumaA HadiyvFA They two (a man and a woman) made soft discourse together, saying that which excited each to feel an eager desire for, or to lust after, the other. (TA from a trad.) ― -b4- xaDaEa , aor. , inf. n. xaDoEN , [or, as in two copies of the S, xaDaEN , though it seems that the verb is correctly xaDaEa , not xaDiEa ,] He had a natural stooping of the neck: (TA:) and he bent himself, or became bent; as also ↓ AxDE . (Zj.) And ↓ AxtDE , said of a hawk, He lowered his head to make a stoop, or to pounce down. (Z, TA.) ― -b5- [Hence,] xaDaEati AlA_ibilu (tropical:) The camels strove, or exerted themselves, or hastened, in their pace, or going; (K;) because, when they do so, they lower their necks. (TA.) And ↓ AxtDE , (K,) said of a horse, (IAar,) [for the same reason,] (assumed tropical:) He went quickly, or swiftly. (IAar, K.) ― -b6- xaDaEa Aln~ajomu (tropical:) The star, or asterism, inclined (S, K, TA) to the place of setting, (S, TA,) or to setting: (K, TA:) and in like manner, xaDaEati Al$~amosu (tropical:) the sun inclined &c.; like xadaEat : (TA:) and xaDaEato A^ayodiY AlkawaAkibi (tropical:) the stars inclined to setting. (Aboo- 'Adnán, TA in art. x$E .) -A2- xaDaEahu He, or it, rendered him still (K, TA) [ and submissive: see 1]: the verb being both intrans. and trans. (TA.) [See also 4.] ― -b2- Also, (K,) inf. n. xaDoEN and xuDuwEN , (TA,) He, or it, caused him to have a stooping neck; as also ↓ AxDEhu ; (K;) i. e., bent him: (TA:) said of old age. (TK.) Jereer says, A^aEad~a A@ll~`hu lil$~uEaraA='i min~iY SawaAEiqa yaxoDaEuwna lahu Alr~iqaAbaA [ God hath prepared, for the poets, from me, thunderbolts which make the necks to stoop to Him ]. (TA.) ― -b3- xaDaEa fulaAnFA A_ilaY Als~awo'api ; in the K AlY Als~uw'i , but the former is the right; inf. n. xuDuwEN ; (TA;) He, or it, invited such a one to that which was foul, abominable, or evil. (K, TA.)

definition: Lowly, humble, or submissive;
sourceDefinition: Lowly, humble, or submissive; (Msb;) and ↓ xaDuwEN signifies the same: (S, K:) [or rather the latter is an intensive epithet, signifying very lowly, &c.:] the pl. of the former is xaADiEuwna and xuD~aEN and xuDoEaAnN , or xiDoEaAnN : (TA:) [respecting the last two of which, see 1, second sentence:] and the pl. of ↓ xaDuwEN is xuDuEN ; (S, K;) as in the phrase qawomN xuDuEu Alr~iqaAbi [ A people, or company of men, very submissive in the necks ]. (S.) It is said in the Kur [xxvi. 3], faZal~ato A^aEonaAquhumo lahaA xaADiEiyna And their necks shall continue, the pret. being used in the sense of the aor., meaning taduwmu , (Jel,) submissive to it: (Jel, * TA:) the original of the phrase is faZal~uwA lahaA xaADiEiyna ; and AEnAq is redundantly inserted to show the place of xuDuwE , and the predicate is left in its original state: (Bd:) or as the xDwE is only that of the AEnAq , it is allowable to make the predicate relate to [the pronoun hm , which is] the complement of the latter word: (Sb, Kh:) or since the xDwE is ascribed to the necks but really belongs to the persons, the epithet has that form of pl. which is proper to rational beings: (Jel: [and the like is said by Bd:]) or AEnAqhm means their chiefs: or their companies: but there is another reading [which is literally grammatical], namely xaADiEapF . (Bd.) ― -b2- The pl. xuD~aEN is also applied to Women who have been [ or who are ] soft in speech, and still. (IAar.) [See 1.] ― -b3- naEaAmN xawaADiEu [pl. of xaADiEapN ] Ostriches inclining their heads towards the ground in their places of pasture; and in like manner, ZibaA='N [ gazelles ]. (TA.) ― -b4- A_ibilN xawaADiEu (tropical:) Camels striving, or exerting themselves, or hastening, in their pace, or going; because, when they do so, they lower their necks. (TA.) ― -b5- manokibN xaADiEN and ↓ A^axoDaEu A low, or depressed, shoulder-joint. (TA.) ― -b6- nujuwmN xawaADiEu (tropical:) Stars inclining to setting, or to their places of setting. (A, TA.) -A2- Inviting to that which is foul, abominable, or evil. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taxoliylN , [ He picked his teeth; ] he extracted the remains of food between his teeth with a xilaAl [or toothpick]; (Msb, K, * in which latter the pass. form of the verb is mentioned;) and so ↓ txl~l , alone; (T, S, * O, TA;) but accord. to the K, you say, txll~`hu [ he extracted it ], meaning the remains of food between the teeth. (TA.) ― -b2- xl~l Al$~aEara biAlmu$oTi [ He separated the hair with the comb; he combed the hair ]. (Mgh voce ta$oriyHN .) ― -b3- xl~l liHoyatahu , (S, * Msb, K,) and A^aSaAbiEahu , (S, * K,) inf. n. as above, (S,) He made the water to flow into the interstices of his beard, (Msb, K,) and of his fingers or toes, (K,) in the ablution termed wuDuwo' ; (S, TA;) and ↓ txl~l , alone, signifies the same. (S.) It (the former) is as though it were taken from taxal~alotu Alqawoma meaning “ I entered amid the breaks, or interspaces, of the people. ” (Msb.) Hence the trad., xal~iluwA A^aSaAbiEakumo laA tuxal~alahaA naArN qaliylN buqoyaAhaA [ Make ye the water to flow into the interstices of your fingers or toes, lest fire that shall spare little be made to flow into their interstices ]. (TA.) ― -b4- xll~`hu kilosFA He put SaAruwj [or kilos , i. e. quick lime, &c.,] into the interstices of its (a building's) stones. (TA in art. kls .) ― -b5- xl~l Alqiv~aA='a , and AlbiT~iyxa , inf. n. as above, He investigated the state of the cucumbers, and the melons, or water-melons, so as to see every one that had not grown, and put another in its place. (AA, TA.) ― -b6- See also 1, in the latter half of the paragraph. -A2- And see 1 again, last sentence. -A3- xl~l , inf. n. taxoliylN , said of wine and of other beverages, It became acid, or sour; and spoiled: (K:) or, said of $araAb [i. e. wine and the like], (Mgh,) or of nabiy* [i. e. must and the like], (Msb,) or of expressed juice, (K,) it became vinegar; (Mgh, Msb, K;) as also ↓ Axtl~ ; (Lth, K;) but this is disallowed by Az; (TA;) and ↓ txl~l ; but this is of the language of the lawyers; (Mgh;) or, said of nby* , this last signifies it was made into vinegar: (Msb:) or xl~l , said of $rAb , signifies it spoiled, (JK, T,) and became vinegar. (T.) -A4- taxoliylN also signifies The making vinegar; (S;) and so ↓ AixotilaAlN ; (K;) i. e. of the expressed juice of grapes and of dates. (TA.) You say, xl~l Alxamora , (K,) or Al$~araAba , (Mgh,) or Aln~abiy* , inf. n. as above, (Msb,) the verb being trans. as well as intrans., (Mgh, Msb, K,) and Aln~abiy*a ↓ txl~l , (TA,) He made the wine, or beverage, or must or the like, into vinegar. (Mgh, Msb, K, TA.) -A5- And xl~l Albusora He put the full-grown unripe dates in the sun, and then sprinkled them ( naDaHahu , in some copies of the K nDjh ,) with vinegar, and placed them in a jar: (K:) so in the M: and in like manner, other things than busor ; as cucumbers, and cabbage, and baA*anojaAn [q. v.], and onions. (TA.) [Accord. to modern usage, the verb signifies He pickled. ]

definition: [primarily signifies It entered, or penetrated, or passed through, the xilaAl , i.
sourceDefinition: [primarily signifies It entered, or penetrated, or passed through, the xilaAl , i. e. interstices, &c., of a thing ]. definition: [primarily signifies] It had interstices, breaks, chinks, or the like.
sourceDefinition: [primarily signifies] It had interstices, breaks, chinks, or the like. (MA. [See xalalN .]) ― -b2- [And hence,] It was, or became, shaky, loose, lax, uncompact, disordered, unsound, corrupt, (Msb,) faulty, or defective, (KL, Msb,) [and weak, or infirm, (see xalalN and muxotal~N ,)] said of a thing or an affair; (KL;) it became altered for the worse. (Msb.) [You say, Axtl~ mizaAjuhu His constitution, or temperament, became in a corrupt or disordered state. And Axtl~ alone He was, or became, disordered in temper; (see taHam~aDa ;) but this seems to be from the same verb said of a camel; (see Axtl~t AlA^ibilu , below;) for the camel becomes disordered in his stomach by pasturing long upon xul~ap , without shifting to HamoD . And Axtl~ Eaqolahu His mind, or intellect, was, or became, unsound, or disordered. ] And Axtl~ A^amoruhu [ His affair, or state, was, or became, unsound, corrupt, or disordered ]; (S, voce AiDoTaraba ;) i. e. waqaEa fiyhi Alxalalu . (JM.) ― -b3- He was, or became, lean, meagre, or emaciated; (KL;) and so Axtl~ jisomuhu . (S.) See 1, first sentence. ― -b4- See also xal~a as syn. with A^axal~a or A^uxil~a &c., near the beginning of the first paragraph. (JK.) -A2- See also 2, in two places. -A3- Axtl~hu biAlr~umoHi , and biAls~ahomi : and yaxotal~u Alv~aworu Alkaloba biqaronihi : see 1, in the former half of the paragraph. ― -b2- Axtl~ also signifies He served together. (KL.) ― -b3- Auxotul~a said of herbage: see xul~apN , near the end of the paragraph. -A4- Axtl~ AlmakaAnu The place had in it xul~ap [q. v.]. (MA.) ― -b2- And Axtl~t AlA_ibilu The camels were confined in [ pasturage such as is termed ] xul~ap . (K.)

definition: a word of well-known meaning, (S, Msb.
sourceDefinition: a word of well-known meaning, (S, Msb.) Vinegar; i. e. expressed juice of grapes (JK, Mgh, K) and of dates (JK) &c. (K) that has become acid, or sour: (JK, * Mgh, K:) so called because its sweet flavour has become altered for the worse ( Aixotal~a ): (Msb:) a genuine Arabic word: (IDrd, K:) the best is that of wine: it is composed of two constituents (K) of subtile natures, (TA,) hot and cold, (K,) the cold being predominant: (TA:) and is good for the stomach; and for the gums, (K,) which it strengthens, when one rinses the mouth with it; (TA;) and for foul ulcers or sores; and for the itch; and for the bite, or sting, of venomous reptiles; and as an antidote for the eating of opium; and for burns; and for toothache; and its hot vapour is good for the dropsy, and for difficulty of hearing, and for ringing in the ears: (K: [various other properties &c. are assigned to it in the TA:]) ↓ xal~apN signifies somewhat (lit. a portion ) thereof; [being the n. un.:] (Aboo-Ziyád, K;) or it may be a dial. var. thereof, like as xamorapN is [said by some to be] of xamorN : (Aboo-Ziyád, TA:) see also xal~apN : the pl. is xuluwlN [meaning sorts, or kinds, of vinegar ]. (Msb.) It is said in a trad., niEoma AlA_idaAmu Alxal~u [ Excellent, or most excellent, is the seasoning, vinegar! ]. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A^um~u Alxal~i [ The mother of vinegar; meaning] wine. (JK, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also the saying,] maA fulaAnN bixal~K walaA xamorK , (A'Obeyd, JK, S,) or maA lahu xal~N walaA xamorN , (K,) or maA Einoda fulaAnK xal~N walaA xamorN , (S, in art. xmr ,) Such a one, or he, possesses neither good nor evil: (A'Obeyd, JK, S, K:) [or neither evil nor good: for] AA says that some of the Arabs make Alxamoru to be good, and Alxal~u to be evil; [and thus the latter is explained in one place, in this art., in the K;] and some of them make Alxmr to be evil, and Alxl~ to be good. (Har p. 153.) -A2- I. q. HamoDN [i. e. A kind of plants in which is saltness: or salt and bitter plants: or salt, or sour, plants or trees: &c.: opposed to xul~apN ]. (K.) A poet says, layosato mina Alxal~i walaA AlximaATi [ She is not, or they are not, of the plants or trees called xl~ , nor of the kind called xmAT (pl. of xamoTN )]. (TA.) -A3- A road in sands: (S:) or a road passing through sands: or a road between two tracts of sand: (K:) or a road passing through heaped-up sands: (JK, K:) masc. and fem. [like TariyqN ]: (S, K:) pl. [of pauc.] A^axol~N and [of mult.] xilaAlN . (K.) One says Hay~apu xal~K [ A serpent of a road in sands, &c.]; like as one says A^afoEaY SariymapK . (S.) ― -b2- An oblong tract of sand. (Ham p. 709.) ― -b3- ― -b4- A vein in the neck (JK, K) and in the back, (K,) communicating with the head. (JK, TA.) ― -b5- A slit, or rent, in a garment, or piece of cloth. (K.) -A4- An old and worn-out garment, or piece of cloth, (JK, S, K, TA,) in which are streaks: (TA:) [or so vawobN xal~N :] and ↓ xaloxalN and ↓ xaloxalN , applied to a garment, or piece of cloth, (JK, K,) signify old and worn out, (JK,) or thin, (K,) like halohalN and halohaAlN . (TA.) ― -b2- A bird having no feathers: (JK:) or having few feathers. (K.) ― -b3- A man (JK, S) lean, meagre, or emaciated; (JK, S, K;) as also ↓ xaliylN (K) [a meaning said in the TA to be tropical] and ↓ maxoluwlN and ↓ muxotal~N : (TA:) or light in body: (IDrd, TA:) and [the fem.] xal~apN , applied to a woman, light (K, TA) in body, lean, or spare: (TA:) the pl. of xal~N is xuluwlN . (JK.) Also Fat: thus bearing two contr. significations: (K:) and so ↓ maxoluwlN . (TA.) It is applied to a man and a camel. (TA.) Accord. to the K, it also signifies A [ young camel such as is termed ] faSiyl : (TA:) but it means such as is lean, or emaciated: (TA:) and so ↓ maxoluwlN , applied to a fSyl as an epithet, for a reason mentioned above, in an explanation of the phrase xal~a AlfaSiyla . (S, TA.) ― -b4- Also i. q. Aibonu maxaADK [i. e. A male camel in his second year ]; (JK, K;) and so ↓ xal~apN ; which is also applied to the female: (As, S, K:) and i. q. Aibonu labuwnK [i. e. a male camel in, or entering upon, his third year ]; and in like manner ↓ xal~apN is applied to the female; (JK;) or, as in the M, to a she-camel; (TA;) and, as some say, (JK,) a large she-camel: (JK, TA:) and Aibonu ↓ Alxal~api signifies the same as Aibonu All~abuwni (T in art. bnY ) or Aibonu maxaADK [or Abn AlmaxaADi ]. (TA in that art.) You say, A^ataAhumo biquroSK kaA^an~ahu firosinu ↓ xal~apK , (S, TA,) or kaA^an~ahu xuf~u xal~apK , (JK,) [ They brought them a round cake of bread as though it were the foot of a camel in its second, or third, year, ] meaning small. (JK. [In the TA, meaning samiynap (i. e. fat ); but this seems to be a mistranscription.]) -A5- A cautery. (TA.)

definition: A road between two roads.
sourceDefinition: A road between two roads. (TA.) ― -b2- A hole, perforation, or bore, that penetrates, or passes through, a thing, and is small: or, in a general sense: (K:) or a gap, or breach, in a booth of reeds or canes. (T, TA.) [See also xalalN .] ― -b3- [And hence,] The gap that is left by a person who has died: (As, T, S, TA:) or the place, of a man, that is left vacant after his death. (K.) One says, of him who has lost a person by death, Aall~`hum~a A@xolufo EalaY A^aholihi bixayorK waA@sodudo xal~atahu , i. e. [ O God, supply to his family, with that which is good, the place of him whom they have lost, ] and fill up the gap which he has left by his death. (As, T, S, * TA.) ― -b4- And The interval, or inter- vening space, between the piercer, or thruster, and the pierced, or thrust: whence the saying, raqaEa xal~apa AlfaArisi , explained in art. rqE . (O and K and TA in that art.) ― -b5- [Hence also,] Want, or a want: poverty; (S, Msb, K;) need, straitness, or difficulty. (Lh, K.) One says, bihi xal~apN $adiydapN He has pressing, or severe, need or straitness or difficulty. (Lh, TA.) And sad~a A@ll~`hu xal~atahu May God supply his want. (TA.) And it is said in a prov., Alxal~apu tadoEuw A_ilaY Als~al~api Want invites to theft. (K, * TA.) -A2- I. q. xaSolapN ; (JK, S, Mgh, Msb, K;) both signify A property, quality, nature, or disposition: and a habit, or custom: (KL, PS, TK:) [and app. also a practice, or an action: ] in a man: (TA: [see the latter word:]) pl. xilaAlN . (JK, Mgh, Msb, K.) One says, fulaAnN xal~atuhu HasanapN [ Such a one, his nature, or disposition, is good ]. (IDrd, TA.) And hence, xayoru xilaAli AlS~aAy^imi Als~iwaAku [ The best of the habits, or customs, of the faster is the use of the tooth-stick ]. (Mgh.) ― -b2- See also xul~apN . -A3- An isolated tract of sand, (Fr, K,) separate from other sands. (Fr, TA.) ― -b2- And i. q. haDobapN [which signifies An elevated tract of sand: but more commonly a hill; or a spreading mountain; &c.]. (JK, TA.) -A4- Wine, (K,) in a general sense: (TA:) or acid, or sour, wine: (S, K:) or wine altered for the worse, (K, TA,) in flavour, (TA,) without acidity, or sourness: (K, TA:) pl. [or coll. gen. n.] ↓ xal~N . (K.) ― -b2- See also xal~N , first sentence. -A5- And see this last word near the end of the paragraph, in four places.

definition: an inf. n. [or rather quasi-inf. n.] of xaAl~ahu , q. v.: (JK:) True, or sincere, friendship, love, or affection; as also ↓ xuluwlapN and ↓ xulaAlapN and ↓ xalaAlapN and ↓ xilaAlapN : (S:) or all...
sourceDefinition: an inf. n. [or rather quasi-inf. n.] of xaAl~ahu , q. v.: (JK:) True, or sincere, friendship, love, or affection; as also ↓ xuluwlapN and ↓ xulaAlapN and ↓ xalaAlapN and ↓ xilaAlapN : (S:) or all these signify a particular true or sincere friendship, or love, or affection, in which is no unsoundness, or defect, and which may be chaste and may be vitious: (K: [in which all are said to be substs., except xul~apN , as though this were properly speaking an inf. n., though having a pl., as shown below:]) [and sometimes simply friendship: see an ex. in a verse cited voce maroHabN , in art. rHb :] or xul~apN and ↓ xal~apN , (Msb,) or ↓ xil~N and ↓ xil~apN , each with kesr, (K,) signify true, or sincere, friendship, or love, or affection, (Msb, K,) and brotherly conduct: the last two as used in the phrases, A_inahu ↓ lakariymu Alxil~i and ↓ Alxil~api [ Verily he is generous in respect of true, or sincere, friendship, &c.]: (K:) the pl. of xul~apN in the sense explained above is xilaAlN . (S, K.) ― -b2- See also xaliylN , in three places. -A2- A kind of plants or herbage [or trees ]; (JK, S, Msb, K;) namely, the sweet kind thereof; (S, K;) not HamoD : (JK:) or any pasture, or herbage, that is not HamoD ; all pasture, or herbage, consisting of HamoD and xul~ap , and HamoD being such as has in it saltness [or sourness]: (TA:) the [ kind of plant, or tree, called ] Earofaj ; and every tree that remains in winter: (JK:) accord. to Lh, it is [applied to certain kinds ] of trees &c.: accord. to IAar, peculiarly of trees: but accord. to A'Obeyd, [ shrubs, i. e.] not including any great trees: (TA:) and a certain thorny tree: also a place of growth, and a place in which is a collection, of [the plants, or trees, called] Earofaj : (K:) and any land not containing [ the kind of plants, or herbage, or trees, called ] HamoD ; (AHn, K;) even though containing no plants, or herbage: (AHn, TA:) the pl. is xulalN : (K:) one says A^aroDN xul~apN and A^araDuwna xulalN : ISh says that A^aroDN xal~apN and xulalu AlA^aroDi mean land, and lands, in which is no HamoD , sometimes containing [ thorny trees such as are called ] EiDaAh , and sometimes not containing such; and that xul~apN is also applied to land in which are no trees nor any herbage: (TA:) some say that xul~apN , as meaning the pasture, or herbage, which is the contrary of HamoD , has for a pl. xilaAlN , and then, from xilaAl is formed the pl. A^axil~apN : and some say that this last means herbage that is cut ( waA@jotuz~ ↓ Auxotul~ [in which the latter verb seems to be an explicative adjunct to the former]) while green. (Ham p. 662, q. v.) They say that the xul~ap is the bread of camels, and the HamoD is their fruit, (JK, T, Sudot;, TA,) or their flesh-meat, (S, TA,) or their xabiyS . (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, by way of comparison, it is applied to (tropical:) Ease, or repose; freedom from trouble or inconvenience, and toil or fatigue; or tranquillity; and ampleness of circumstances: and HamoD , to evil, and war: (T, TA:) and the former, to life: and the latter, to death. (Ham p. 315.) ― -b3- Also Acid, or sour, leaven or ferment. (IAar, TA.)

definition: An interstice, an interspace or intervening space, a break, a breach, a chink, or a gap, between two things;
sourceDefinition: An interstice, an interspace or intervening space, a break, a breach, a chink, or a gap, between two things; (JK, S, Msb, K;) pl. xilaAlN : (JK, S, Msb:) and particularly the places, (K,) or interstices, (S,) of the clouds, from which the rain issues; as also ↓ xilaAlN ; (S, K;) both occurring in this sense, accord. to different readings, in the Kur xxiv. 43 and xxx. 47: (S, TA:) the latter may be [grammatically] a sing. [syn. with the former], or it may be pl. of the former: (MF, TA:) and Ald~aAri ↓ xilaAlu signifies what is around the limits of the house; (JK, K;) or around the walls thereof; thus in the M; (TA;) and what is between the chambers thereof. (K.) You say, daxalotu bayona xalali Alqawomi and ↓ xilaAlihimo [ I entered amid the breaks, or interspaces, of the people ]. (S, Msb.) And huwa xalalahumo and ↓ xilaAlahumo (M, K) and ↓ xalaAlahumo (K [but in the CK these words are with damm to the second l ]) He is amid them. (M, K.) And buyuwti AlH~Y ↓ jusonaA xilaAla , and duwri Alqawomi ↓ xilaAla , i. e. [ We went, or went to and fro, or went round about, &c., ] amid the tents of the tribe, and in the midst of the houses of the people; like a phrase in the Kur xvii. 5. (TA.) ― -b2- And [hence] Shakiness, looseness, laxness, or want of compactness, and disorder, or want of order, of a thing; (Msb;) unsoundness, or corruptness, (S, Msb, *) in an affair or a thing, (S,) or of a thing; (Msb;) [ a flaw in a thing;] defect, imperfection, or deficiency; (Ham p. 300;) weakness, or infirmity, in an affair, (JK, K, TA,) as though some place thereof were left uncompact, or unsound, (TA,) and in war, (JK,) and in men: (JK, K: *) and (tropical:) unsettledness in an opinion. (K, * TA.) ― -b3- Alxalalu The night. (JK, Ibn- 'Abbád.)

definition: Perforated, or transpierced;
sourceDefinition: Perforated, or transpierced; like ↓ maxoluwlN . (K.) ― -b2- See also xal~N , in the latter half of the paragraph. ― -b3- Poor; needy; in want; (JK, S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ muxil~N , (so in some copies of the K and in the M,) or ↓ muxal~N , (so in other copies of the K,) and ↓ muxotal~N and ↓ A^axal~u (K:) and A^axil~apN may be a pl. of xaliylN in this sense. (Ham p. 662.) ― -b4- A friend; or a true, or sincere, friend; (S, Mgh, Msb;) as also ↓ xil~N , and ↓ xul~apN , which is used alike as masc. and fem., because originally an inf. n., [or a quasi-inf. n., i. e. of 3, q. v.,] (S,) or ↓ xil~apN , [thus in the copies of the K, but what precedes it, though not immediately, seems to show that the author perhaps meant xul~apN ,] used alike as masc. and fem. and sing. and pl.: (K:) or a special, or particular, friend or true or sincere friend; as also ↓ xil~N and ↓ xul~N ; or this latter is only used in conjunction with wud~N , as when you say, kaAna liY wud~FA waxul~FA [ He was to me an an object of love and a friend &c.]; (K;) or, as ISd says, ↓ xil~N is the more common, and is applied also to a female; (TA;) as is also ↓ xul~apN , (K,) and ↓ xil~apN : (TA:) xaliylN also signifies veracious; (K;) thus accord. to IAar: (TA:) or a friend in whose friendship is no xalal [i. e. unsoundness, or defect, or imperfection ]: (Zj, TA:) or one who is pure and sound in friendship, or love: (IDrd, K:) the pl. is A^axil~aA='u (Msb, K) and xul~aAnN (JK, K) and A^axil~apN : (Ham p. 662, and MA:) the fem. is xaliylapN ; (S, M, K;) of which the pl. is xaliylaAtN and xalaAy^ilu : (M, K:) the pl. of ↓ xil~N or ↓ xul~N is A^axolaAlN : (K:) and the pl. of ↓ xul~apN is xilaAlN , (S,) mentioned before, see 3, second sentence. It is applied in the Kur iv. 124 to Abraham; who is called xaliylu A@ll~`h , (TA,) and Alxaliylu . (K.) And it is said that the pl. A^axil~apN means also Pastors; because they act to their beasts like A^axil~aA=' [or friends, &c.], in labouring to do good to them. (Ham p. 662.) ― -b5- Also One who advises, or counsels, or acts, sincerely, honestly, or faithfully. (IAar, TA.) ― -b6- And Alxaliylu also signifies The heart. (IAar, JK, K.) ― -b7- And The liver. (JK, TA.) ― -b8- And The nose. (JK, K.) ― -b9- And The sword. (IAar, TA.) [And] A sword of Sa'eed Ibn-Zeyd Ibn-' Amr Ibn-Nufeyl. (K.) ― -b10- And The spear. (IAar, TA.)

sourceDefinition: aor. , inf. n. dabiybN (T, S, M, Msb, K, &c.) and dab~N (M, K,) and madab~N , (S, K,) [and perhaps dababN also, q. v.,] It, or he, (the ant, T, M, and any animal, M, and in like manner a party moving towards the enemy, T, or an army, and a child, Msb,) [ crept; crawled; or] went, or walked, leisurely, or gently, (T, M, Msb, K,) without haste, (T,) EalaY AlA^aroDi [ upon the ground ]: (S:) and [simply] he walked: (IAar, T:) he (an old man) [ crept along; or] walked leisurely, softly, or gently: (S:) and ↓ db~b , also, he walked leisurely, by slow degrees. (TA.) Hence, A^ako*abu mano dab~a wadaraja The most lying of those who have walked and died, or passed away, or perished: (T:) i. e., of the living and the dead. (T, S, K.) And yadib~u maEa AlquraAdi [ He creeps about with ticks ]; said of a man who brings a small worn-out skin containing ticks, and ties it to the tail of a camel; in consequence of which, when one of the ticks bites it, the camel runs away, and the other camels run away with it; and thereupon he steals one of them: whence it is said of a thief, or stealer of cattle &c. (TA.) And huwa yadib~u bayonanaA biAln~amaAy^imi (tropical:) [ He creeps among us with calumnies, or slanders ]. (A, TA.) And dab~ato EaqaArabuhu [lit. His scorpions crept along ]; meaning (tropical:) his calumnies, or slanders, and mischief, (M, A, K,) crept along; syn. sarato . (M, K [See also art. Eqrb .]) And the same phrase is also used to signify (tropical:) His downy hair crept [ along his cheeks ]. (MF in art. Eqrb .) And dab~a qamoluhu [lit. His lice crept ]; meaning (tropical:) he became fat: said of a man. (Ham. p. 633.) And dab~a Aljadowalu (tropical:) [ The rivulet, or streamlet for irrigation, crept along ]. (A.) And dab~a fiyhi (tropical:) It crept in, or into, it, or him; syn. saraY ; (M, A, K;) namely, wine, or beverage, (T, M, A, K,) in, or into, the body, (M, K,) or in, or into, a man, (T,) and into a vessel; (M;) and a disease, or malady, (M, A, K,) in, or into, the body, (M, K,) or fiY Euruwqihi [ in his veins ]; (A;) and wear in a garment, or piece of cloth; (M, K;) and the dawn in the darkness of the latter part of the night. (M.) ― -b2- dib~iY Hajalo (in the CK Hajalu ) is the name of A certain game of the Arabs: (K, TA:) the l is quiescent. (TA.) ― -b3- dub~a used as a noun: see below. -A2- dab~a [second pers. dabibota ,] aor. yadab~u , inf. n. dababN , He (a camel) was, or became, such as is termed A^adab~u ; (IAar, T, TA;) i. e., had much hair, or much fur ( wabar ), or much fur upon the face. (TA.)

for which, if it applied only to an irrational creature, faminohaA or faminohun~a would be used: moreover, the expression mn ym$Y is used, though dAb~p applies originally to an irrational creature, [or rather a beast, and a reptile, ] because the different classes of beings are spoken of collectively: (M:) and this passage of the Kur refutes the assertion of him who excludes the bird from the significations of this word: (Msb:) in the last verse but one of ch. xxxv. of the Kur, it is said to relate to mankind and the jinn (or genii) and every rational being; or to have a general signification: (M:) its predominant signification is a beast that is ridden: (S, M, A, K:) especially a beast of the equine kind; i. e. a horse, a mule, and an ass: (Kull:) or particularly a biro*awon [meaning hackney, or horse for ordinary use and for journeying: (M:) but as particularly applied, when used absolutely, to a horse and a mule, it is an adventitious conventional term: (Msb:) it is applied to a male and a female: (M, A, Msb, K:) and is properly an epithet: (M:) pl. dawaAb~u . [signifying Any small animal that walks or creeps or crawls upon the earth, a small beast, a small reptile or creeping thing, a creeping insect, and any insect, and also a mollusk, a shell-fish (as in an instance cited voce maHaArapN in art. sourceDefinition: , (T, S, M, K,) also termed davay^iY~N , (As, IAar, S, K,) but this latter is not of established authority, and is not mentioned in the M nor in the O., (TA in art. dvA^ ,) The rain that falls after the heat has acquired strength; (M, K in art. dvA^ , TA;) when the earth has put (lit. vomited ) forth the kamoA^ap [or truffles, which, accord. to Kzw, are found in Nejd (Central Arabia) at the period of the auroral setting of the Tenth Mansion of the Moon, (which happened, about the commencement of the era of the Flight, in that part, on the 11th of February O. S.,) when the sharpness of winter is broken, and the trees put forth their leaves: see also 1 in art. ntj ]: (Lth, IAar, Th, M:) or the rain that is after [ that called ] the rabiyE [q.v.], before, ( qabol , as in one copy of the S, in another qbl without any syll. signs,) or in the first part of, ( qubul , as in the TA,) [ that called ] the Sayof [q. v., see also nawo'N ], when the kamoA^ap disappear entirely from the earth: (S, O, TA:) AZ says that the beginning of the dafay^iY~ is wuquwEu Aljabohapi and the end is AlS~rofapu [i. e. the period extends from the auroral setting of the Tenth Mansion of the Moon ( about the 11th of February O. S. as explained above, when the sun in Arabia has begun to have much power,) to about the 9th of March O. S.: see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl ; and see also another statement voce nawo'N ]. (S, TA.) ― -b2- And the term ↓ dafay^iy~apN [used as a subst., or as an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant, for miyrapN dafay^iy~apN ,] is applied to The miyrap [or provision of corn &c. ], (AZ, T, S, M, K,) whatever it be, that is brought (AZ, T, S) before, ( qbl , written without any syll. signs in a copy of the S, and qbla in the CK,) or in the first part of, ( qubul , as in the M and TA and in a copy of the S and in one of the K, [and this appears to be the right reading,] in a copy of the T qibl ,) the Sayof [here meaning spring ]: (AZ, T, S, M, K:) this is the third myrp ; [see this word for an explanation of the statement here given;] the first being that called the riboEiy~ap [q. v.]; and the second, that called the Sayofiy~ap [q. v.]: then comes the dfy^y~p ; and then, the ramaDiy~ap , which comes when the earth becomes burnt [by the sun]. (M.) ― -b3- And in like manner also, (AZ, S,) i. e., by the term dafay^iY~N is also meant, (M,) The nitaAj [or offspring ] (AZ, S, M) of sheep or goats [ brought forth at that period, as is implied in the S, or] in the end of winter: or, as some say, at any time. (M.)

sourceDefinition: Calamity, or misfortune; (JK, S, K;) as also A^um~u Ald~uhayomi ; (S, K;) and ↓ Ald~uhayomaA='u , (JK, S,) dim. of Ald~ahomaA='u [fem. of AlA^adohamu ], so called because of its darkness: (S, TA:) or Ald~ahayomaA='u signifies black, dark, trial or conflict and faction or sedition or the like; and the dim. form is used to denote enhancement: (Sh, TA:) and ↓ Ald~ahomaA='u signifies black, dark, calamity or misfortunes: (TA:) calamity, or misfortune, is termed Ald~uhayomu because of its darkness: (TA:) or, originally, (S,) this was the name of the she-camel of 'Amr Ibn-Ez-Zebbán Edh-Dhuhlee, who was slain, with his brothers, and their heads were put upon her, (S, K, TA,) in sacks hung upon her neck, and she returned to Ez-Zebbán: (TA:) whence the saying, A^avoqalu mino Himoli Ald~uhayomi [ Heavier than the burden of Ed-Duheym ]: (S:) and A^a$oA^amu mina Ald~uhayomi [ More unlucky than Ed-Duheym ]: (S, K, TA:) or, as some say, seven brothers were slain in a warring and plundering expedition, and were put upon Ed-Duheym; and hence the name became proverbial as applied to any calamity or misfortune. (TA.) -A2- duhayomN also signifies Foolish, or stupid. (K.)

definition: Black; (JK, S, * Mgh, Msb, * K;) as also ↓ duhaAmN : (K:) the former is applied in this sense to a horse, (S, * Mgh, Msb, * TA,) and to a camel, &c.: (TA:) or, applied to a camel, of a deep ashcolour...
sourceDefinition: Black; (JK, S, * Mgh, Msb, * K;) as also ↓ duhaAmN : (K:) the former is applied in this sense to a horse, (S, * Mgh, Msb, * TA,) and to a camel, &c.: (TA:) or, applied to a camel, of a deep ashcolour without any tinge of white; (As, S, Msb, K;) when of a deeper hue, so as to be very black, he is termed jawonN : (S:) or, as some say, applied to a camel, like A^aSofaru , [in this case meaning black with some intermixture of yellow, ] but less black: (TA:) fem. dahomaA='u ; which, when applied to a sheep (S, M, Msb, K) or goat, (S, Msb,) means of a pure or an unmixed brown colour ( xaAliSapu AlHumorapi ): (S, M, Msb, K:) pl. duhomN . (TA.) The Arabs say, muluwku Alxayoli duhomuhaA [ The kings of horses are the black thereof ]. (TA.) And farasN A^adohamu bahiymN A black horse in which is no intermixture of colours. (TA.) And laA A=tiyka maA Han~ati Ald~ahomaA='u [ I will not come to thee as long as she (among the camels) that is of a deep ash-colour without any tinge of white reiterates her yearning cry after her young one; meaning, ever ]. (Lh, TA.) And ramaAdN A^adohamu Black ashes. (TA.) ― -b2- HadiyqapN dahomaA='u and ↓ mudohaAm~apN (tropical:) [ A walled garden ] green inclining to black. (K.) Hence, (K,) ↓ mudohaAm~ataAni , (S, K,) in the Kur [lv. 64], (S, TA,) [ Two gardens ( jan~ataAni )] of which the greenness inclines to blackness; for every green plant, when its abundance and its moisture, or irrigation, are complete, inclines to blackness: (Zj, TA:) or black by reason of intense greenness arising from abundant moisture, or irrigation; and everything that is green ( A^axoDar ) the Arabs term A^asowadu . (S, TA.) ― -b3- raboEN A^adohamu [ A place of alighting or abode ] recently occupied by the tribe; [because blackened by their fires &c.:] pl. A^arobuEN duhomN . (TA.) And A^avarN A^adohamu A new, or recent, mark, trace, or vestige: (As, K:) and A^agoyaru means one that is “old, becoming effaced:” (As, TA:) and the former means also old, becoming effaced; (K;) as some explain it; (TA;) thus having two contr. significations. (K.) And waToA^apN dahomaA='u A new, or recent, footstep, or footprint: and gaboraA='u means “becoming effaced:” or the former means one that is becoming effaced, because it has become obscure to him who seeks it; (JK;) or an old footstep, or footprint: and HamoraA='u means one that is “new, or recent.” (S.) [See also A^agobaru .] ― -b4- Ald~ahomaA='u also signifies (tropical:) The cooking-pot: (JK, S, A, K:) or the black cooking-pot: (ISh, TA:) and the old cooking-pot. (K. [But it is implied in the TA that this last meaning is a mistake, occasioned by an omission; and that, instead of Alqidoru waAlqadiymapu , (in the CK Alqidoru Alqadiymapu ,) we should read, Alqidoru waAlwaToA^apu Ald~ahomaA='u Alqadiymapu , explained above. Accord. to Golius, on the authority of a gloss in the KL, A^abuw AlA^adohami signifies The great cooking-pot in which a whole sheep is cooked at once. ]) ― -b5- And The twenty-ninth night of the [ lunar ] month: (JK, K:) because of its blackness. (TA.) And [the pl.] Ald~uhomu Three nights of the [ lunar ] month [ during which is the change of the moon ]: (K:) because they are black. (TA.) ― -b6- See also Ald~uhayomu . ― -b7- [Used as a subst.,] A^adohamu signifies also A shackle or fetter, or a pair of shackles or fetters; syn. qayodN : (S, K:) because of the blackness thereof: accord. to AA, of wood: (TA:) or a heavy shackle or fetter or a pair of shackles or fetters: syn. A^adaAhimu : (S, K:) because of the blackform of pl., which is proper to substs., because the quality of a subst. is predominant in it. (TA.) ― -b8- And [the fem.] dahomaA='u signifies (assumed tropical:) A multitude, or large number: (K:) and (assumed tropical:) a company of men; (Ks, S, K; *) and multitude thereof: (Ks, TA:) or (tropical:) the generality, the common mass, or the main part [thereof]: (Z, TA:) or (assumed tropical:) the commonalty, or common people. (Mbr, Har p. 671.) [See also dahomN .] -A2- Also, dahomaA='u , The aspect, appearance, mien, guise, or garb, of a man. (JK, S, * K.) -A3- And Ald~ahomaA='u A certain herb, or tree, green, and broad in the leaves; (JK;) or a certain broad herb, (K,) having leaves and twigs, resembling the qaronuwap ; (TA;) with which one tans. (JK, K.)

(T, S, M, K) and , (S, M, K,) inf. n. *aborN ; (M, A, K;) and ↓ *b~r , (M, A,) inf. n. ta*obiyrN ; (K;) He wrote (A 'Obeyd, T, S, M, A, K) a writing, or a book; (A 'Obeyd, T, S, M, A;) like zabara : (A 'Obeyd, T, S:) or both signify, (M,) or the former signifies also, (K,) he pointed, or dotted, (M, K,) it: (M:) or (M, but in the K “ and, ”) he read it, or recited it, (IAar, T, M, K, *) with a low, or faint, voice; (M, K;) or easily; (M, A, each in relation to both verbs;) or quickly: (K:) all of the dial. of Hudheyl. (M.) You say, maA A^aHosana maA ya*oburu Al$~iEora How well he recites poetry, or the poetry, (K, TA,) without halting, or hesitating, therein! (TA.) And AlkitaAba ↓ maA A^aHosana maA yu*ab~iru How well he reads, or recites, the book, or the writing, without pausing therein! (A.) ― -b2- And *abara , (IAar, Th, T, M, K,) aor. , inf. n. *aborN and *ibaArapN , He knew, or learned, a tradition, well, soundly, or thoroughly; Eanohu from him: (IAar, Th, T:) or he understood it: (M, K:) and he understood, and knew, or learned, well, soundly, or thoroughly, a writing, or a book. (TA.) [See 2 in art. dbr , last sentence.] Accord. to some, *aborN signifies Understanding, and knowledge; (T;) knowledge of a thing, and understanding thereof; (K, * TA;) as also *ubuwrN [another inf. n.] : (TA:) or *ubuwrN signifies understanding with knowledge of a thing. (M.) It is said in a trad., of the people of Paradise, minohumo Al~a*iY laA *abora lahu , (T, TA,) i. e. Of them is he who has no understanding: (TA:) or, accord. to IAar, it means he who has no tongue with which to speak, by reason of his weakness. (T.) ― -b3- And *abara , aor. , (K,) inf. n. *ibaArapN , (so in some copies of the K,) or *abaArapN , (so in other copies of the K, and accord. to the TA,) He looked, and did so well. (K, * TA.) -A2- *abira He was angry: (T, K:) so accord. to IAar: (T, TA:) [but SM says,] were it not set down on his authority, I should say that it is a mistranscription for *ay^ira . (TA.)

definition: A number of camels, from three to ten: (Lth, AZ, As, T, S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) this is the meaning that is of best repute: (TA:) [in this explanation in the T from AZ, and in the K, the nouns of number are mase.
sourceDefinition: A number of camels, from three to ten: (Lth, AZ, As, T, S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) this is the meaning that is of best repute: (TA:) [in this explanation in the T from AZ, and in the K, the nouns of number are mase.; and so in the next here following: in the rest, fem.:] or from three to ten: and a little more: (IAar, M:) or from three to nine: (M, L:) or from three to fifteen: or from three to twenty; (M, L, K;) and a little more: (L:) or from three to thirty: (M, L, K:) or from two to nine: (M, Mgh, L, K:) [said to be] applied only to females: (Lth, A'Obeyd, T, M, Mgh, Msb, K:) so in the Bári': (Msb:) and it is of the fem. gender; (T, S, M, Msb, K;) i. e., the word is fem.: (MF:) but its dim. is [↓ *uwayodN ,] without p ; contr. to analogy: (M:) the word *awodN is a pl., (M, K,) meaning a quasipl. n., (MF,) having no sing. (S, M, K) of the same root: (S:) or a sing.; (K;) and its pl. is A^a*owaAdN : (T, S, M, A, Msb, K:) or a sing. and pl.: (M, K:) the Arabs said valaAvu A^a*owaAdK and valaAvu *awodK and so with all the inferior ns. of number, making *awod a substitute for A^a*owaAd : and they also said valaAvu *awodK meaning thereby three she-camels. (M, L.) It is said in a trad., layosa fiymaA duwna xamosi *awodK mina AlA_ibili SadaqapN , (T, L,) or layosa fiYA^aqal~a mino xamosK *awodK SadaqapN , (T, Msb,) meaning [ There is not in the case of less than five ] camels [ any poorrate ]: for the poor-rate is incumbent on him who possesses five camels whether they be males or females. (L.) And in another trad. it is said, fiY xamosi *awodK $aApN [ In the case of five camels, a sheep or goat shall be given]. (Mgh.) And it is said in a prov., Al*~awodu A_ilaY Al*~awodi A_ibilN [ A few she-camels with a few she-camels are a herd of camels ]; (T, S, M, A;) meaning that a little with a little is much; AlY being here used in the sense of maEa : (S, A:) or AlY is here used in its proper sense; a word signifying “ joined ” or the like being understood; (TA;) i. e. a few joined to a few becomes much: (M:) [or,] accord. to the K [and the T], this prov. shows that *wd is here used in the place of AivonataAni [i. e. two she-camels]; for two added to two are a pl.; but this requires consideration. (MF.)

And it is said in a prov., Al*~awodu A_ilaY Al*~awodi A_ibilN [ A few she-camels with a few she-camels are a herd of camels ]; (T, S, M, A;) meaning that a little with a little is much; AlY being here used in the sense of maEa : (S, A:) or AlY is here used in its proper sense; a word signifying “ joined ” or the like being understood; (TA;) i. e. a few joined to a few becomes much: (M:) [or,] accord. to the K [and the T], this prov. shows that *wd is here used in the place of AivonataAni [i. e. two she-camels]; for two added to two are a pl.; but this requires consideration. (MF.)

definition: -A2- Also A certain small animal, resembling the cat.
sourceDefinition: : see riboHN in two places. -A2- Also A certain small animal, resembling the cat. (So in many copies of the S.) F observes that J says, Alr~abaAHu duwayob~apN yujolabu minohaA AlkaAfuwru ; and that baladN has been substituted as an amendment for dwyb~p in some of the copies [of the S]; but that each of these readings is erroneous: for yjlb we find [in copies of the S] in the handwriting of Aboo-Zekereeyà and that of Aboo-Sahl yuHolabu , with the unpointed H ; and the substitution of bld for dwybap was made by IKtt: in the copies of the S, moreover, we find minohu instead of minohaA : and IB says that the passage in J's original copy, in his own handwriting, runs thus: Alr~abaAHu A^ayoDFA duwayob~apN kaAls~in~awri yujolabu minohu AlkaAfuwru . (TA.) [But I find that, in five copies of the S, between Alsn~wr and yjlb , occur the words waAlr~abaAHu A^ayoDFA baladN , or balodapN or A@somu baladK : and I think it most probable that J intended to have introduced these or similar words, and therefore wrote minohu instead of minohaA ; meaning that rbAH is the appellation of a certain small animal, resembling the cat: and that AlrbAH is also the name of a country or town from which camphor is brought: this country or town is said in a marginal note in a copy of the S to be in India.]

Animalium" &c., p. iii.:)] or the young one of an ape: (TA:) or apes [as a coll. gen. n.]: (TA in art. nSH , in explanation of the last, which is there said to be originally rubaAHN :) pl. of the first rabaAbiyHu . (TA.) One says A^amolaHu mino rub~aAHK and rubaAHK , meaning [ Prettier ] than the ape. (A, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence, app.,] rub~u rub~aAHK (Lth, A, K) or rubaAHK (A) A sort of dates (Lth, A, K) of ElBasrah. (Lth.) ― -b3- Also, (K,) accord. to some, (TA,) rub~aAHN signifies A small young weaned camel, (K,) and small young camels, syn. HaA$iyapN , (TA,) slender in the bones and meagre in the body: (K:) but A Heyth asks, How can it mean small young weaned camels, seeing that a poet applies to it the epithet vaniY~ , and the vnY~ is five years old? and Khidásh Ibn-Zuheyr, in a verse cited by Sh, speaks of a rb~AH breathing hard in labour, in order that her young one might come forth. (TA.) ― -b4- See also rubaHN .

definition: (S, M, K) and ↓ ratiymN (M, K) and ↓ marotuwmN (S, K) signify the same;
sourceDefinition: (S, M, K) and ↓ ratiymN (M, K) and ↓ marotuwmN (S, K) signify the same; i. e. Broken: (S, M, K:) and bruised, or crushed, (M, K, TA,) much: (M, and so accord. to the CK:) the first being an inf. n. used as an epithet. (M, K.) Ows Ibn-Hajar says, laA^aSabaHa ratomFA duqaAqa AlHaSaY makaAna Aln~abiY~i mina AlkaAvibi (S, in the present art.,) i. e. It (referring to a mountain called AlSaAqib ) would become [ broken, having the pebbles crushed, ] like the sands around the mountain El-Káthib. (S in art. nbw . [But there are other explanations of AlnbY~ and AlkAvb as here used. In the T, in art. rvm , a different reading is given: lASbH ravomFA .]) -A2- See also ratiymapN . ― -b2- [Freytag, misled by the CK, has assigned to ratomN a signification that belongs to ratamN .]

definition: [applied in the present day to The shrub broom;
sourceDefinition: [applied in the present day to The shrub broom; to several species thereof: spartium monospermum of Linn.: genista rætam of Forsk.: (Delile, Flor. Aegypt. Illustr., no. 657:) spartium: (Forskål, Flora Aegypt. Arab., p. lvi.:) and phalaris setacea: (Idem, p. lx.:)] a species of plant: (T:) or a species of tree; (Mgh;) or so ↓ ratamapN ; of which the former is the pl. [or rather coll. gen. n.]: (S:) or the latter, (Lth, T,) or the former, (AHn, M, K,) the latter being its n. un., (K,) a certain plant, of the shrub-kind; (AHn, T, M, K;) as though by reason of its slenderness, it were likened to the thread, or string, called ratami : (AHn, T, * K, * TA: [see this word voce ratiymapN : in the CK, in the present instance, erroneously written raqom :]) and so ↓ ratiymapN : (AHn, T:) its flower is like the xiyriY~ [or yellow gilliflower ], and its seed is like the lentil: each of these (i. e. the flower and the seed, TA) strongly provokes vomiting: the drinking the expressed juice of its twigs, fasting, is a beneficial remedy for sciatica ( Eiroqu Aln~asaA ); and likewise the using as a clyster an infusion thereof in sea-water: and the swallowing twenty-one grains thereof, fasting, prevents the [ pustules called ] damaAmiyl . (K.) When a man was about to make a journey, he betook himself to two branches, or two trees, and tied one branch to another, and said, “ If my wife be faithful to the compact, this will remain tied as it is; otherwise, she will have broken the compact: ” so says As; and ISk says the like: (T:) or he betook himself to a tree, (S, K,) or to the species of tree called ratam , (ISk, Mgh,) and tied together two branches thereof, (ISk, S, Mgh, K,) or he tied together two trees; (M;) and if he returned and found them as he tied them, he said that his wife had not been unfaithful to him; but otherwise, that she had been so: (ISk, S, M, Mgh, K:) this [ pair of branches or trees ] is called Alr~atamu [in the CK, erroneously, Alr~atomu ] and ↓ Alr~atiymapu : (K:) or this is what is meant by ↓ Alr~atiymapu : (M:) or this [action] is what is meant by taEoqaAdu Alr~atami in the following verse: (As, ISk, T, Mgh:) but IB says that Alr~ataAy^imu [pl. of ↓ Alr~atiymapu ] does not mean peculiarly one kind of trees exclusively of others: and he cites this verse as an ex. of Alr~atamu meaning the threads, or strings, so called; (TA;) as does AZ. (Mgh.) A rájiz says, halo yanofaEanoka Alyawoma A_ino ham~ato bihimo kavorapu maA tuwSiY wataEoqaAdu Alr~atamo [ Will the muchness of thine enjoining, and the tying of the retem, be indeed of use to thee to-day, if she be desirous of them? ]. (T, S, Mgh.) ― -b2- See also ratiymapN , in two places. -A2- Also A [ leathern water-bag such as is called ] mazaAdap that is filled (IAar, T, K) with water: (IAar, T:) or a [ water-skin such as is called ] mazaAd . (M, TT.) -A3- And A road, or way; or the middle, or main part and middle, thereof; or a beaten track; syn. maHaj~apN . (IAar, T, K.) -A4- And Suppressed, low-sounding, occult, or secret, speech or language. (IAar, T, K.) -A5- And Perfect shame or sense of shame or pudency. (IAar, T, K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. raHolN , (S, Msb,) [ He saddled the camel; ] he bound, (S, Mgh, Msb,) or put, (M, K,) the raHol upon the camel; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) as also ↓ ArtHlhu . (K.) And raHalahu raHolahu He bound upon him his apparatus. (TA.) ― -b2- Also, aor. and inf. n. as above, He mounted the camel: (T, TA:) and AlbaEiyra ↓ AirotaHalotu I rode the camel, either with a qatab [or saddle ] or upon his bare back. (Sh, TA.) ― -b3- [Both of these verbs are also used tropically.] You say, raHalotu lahu nafosiY [lit. I saddled for him myself; ] meaning (assumed tropical:) I endured patiently his annoyance, or molestation. (S.) And raHala fulaAnN SaAHibahu bimaA yakorahu (assumed tropical:) [ Such a one put upon, or did to, his companion that which he disliked, or hated ]. (TA.) And [in like manner] ↓ trH~lhu means rakibahu bimakoruwhK (tropical:) [ He did to him an evil, or abominable, or odious, deed ]. (K, TA.) And raHalahu bisayofihi (tropical:) He smote him with his sword. (K, TA.) ― -b4- And raHala fulaAnN fulaAnFA (assumed tropical:) Such a one mounted upon the back of such a one; as also EalaY Zahorihi ↓ ArtHlhu ; [and ArtHlhu alone; for] it is said in a trad., ↓ A_in~a A@boniY A@rotaHalaniY , meaning (assumed tropical:) Verily my son mounted upon my back, making me like the raAHilap : (TA:) and if a man throws down another prostrate, and sits upon his back, you say, raA^ayotuhu murotaHilahu (assumed tropical:) [ I saw him sitting upon his back ]. (Sh, TA.) And [hence] ↓ ArtHl AlA^amora (assumed tropical:) He embarked in the affair. (TA.) And fulaAnN A^amorFA maA yuTiyquhu ↓ ArtHl (assumed tropical:) [ Such a one embarked, or has embarked, in an affair which he is unable to accomplish ]. (TA.) And AlHum~aY ↓ AirotaHalatohu (assumed tropical:) [ The fever continued upon him ]; a phrase similar to rakibatohu AlHm~Y and AimotaTatohu and A^agobaTatohu . (A and TA in art. gbT .) -A2- raHala (S, Mgh, Msb, K) Eani AlmakaAni , (TA,) or Eani Albaladi , (Mgh, Msb,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. raHolN , (TA,) or raHiylN , (Msb,) or this latter is a simple subst.; (S, K, TA;) and ↓ ArtHl , and ↓ triH~l , (S, Msb, K,) Eani AlmakaAni , (K,) or Eani Alqawomi ; (Msb;) all signify the same; (S, Msb;) He removed, (Mgh, K, TA,) went, went away, departed, went forth, or journeyed, (Mgh, TA,) from the place, (K, TA,) or from the country or the like, (Mgh, Msb,.) or from the people. (Msb.) See an ex. of the first of these verbs in a verse cited in the next paragraph. ↓ ArtHl said of a camel, (K,) or ArtHl raHolahu , (TA,) signifies He journeyed, and went away: (K, TA:) [or he had his saddle put upon him: ] and hence, ↓ ArtHl Alqawomu The people, or party, removed. (TA.) ― -b2- raHala bihi : see 2.

sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. taroHiylN ; (K;) and ↓ A^aroHalotuhu (Mgh;) I made him to remove, to go, go away, go forth, or journey, (S, Mgh, Msb, * K, *) from his place; and sent him [ away ]: (S:) and [in like manner] bihi ↓ raHala he made him to remove, go away, depart, or journey: (L in art. x*rf :) and ↓ AlAirotiHaAlu [if not a mistranscription for AlA_iroHaAlu ] signifies the making [one] to go, go away, depart, go forth, or journey; and the removing from one's place. (TA.) A poet says, Al$~ayobu Eano daArK yaHul~u bihaA ↓ laA yaroHalu Hat~aY yuraH~ala EanohaA SaAHibu Ald~aAri [(assumed tropical:) Hoariness will not depart from a dwelling in which it alights until the owner of the dwelling be made to depart from it ]. (TA.) And it is said in a trad. that, at the approach of the hour [of resurrection], Aln~aAsa ↓ taxoruju naArN mino Eadana turoHilu , i.e. [ A fire shall issue from 'Adan ] that shall remove with the people when they remove, and alight with them when they alight: so says EshShaabee; or, Sh says, as some relate it, turaH~ilu Aln~aAsa , i.e. that shall make the people to alight at the maraAHil [or stations ]: or, as some say, that shall make the people to remove, or depart. (TA.) -A2- taroHiylN also signifies The figuring, or embellishing, of garments or cloths [ with the forms of riHaAl , or camels' saddles: see muraH~alN ]. (TA.)

definition: He broke, or trained, a she-camel, so that she became such as is termed raAHilap , meaning fit to be saddled;
sourceDefinition: He broke, or trained, a she-camel, so that she became such as is termed raAHilap , meaning fit to be saddled; (K;) like A^amohara meaning “ he (a breaker, or trainer,) rendered ” her “ a mahoriy~ap : ” (TA:) or he took a camel in an untractable state and rendered him such as is termed raAHilap . (AZ, TA.) ― -b2- And ArHlhu He gave him a raAHilap , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) that he might ride it. (TA.) ― -b3- See also 2, in two places. -A2- He (a camel) became strong in his back, [ so as to be fit for the raHol (or saddle ) or for journeying, ] after weakness: (IDrd, K:) or he (a camel) became fat; as though there came [what resembled] a raHol upon his back, by reason of his fatness and his [large] hump: (Er-Rághib, TA:) and ArHlt AlA_ibilu The camels became fat after leanness, so as to be able to journey. (S K.) ― -b2- And He (a man, TA) had many [ camels such as are termed ] rawaAHil [pl. of raAHilapN ]; (ISd, K;) like A^aEoraba meaning “ he had horses such as are termed EiraAb ” (ISd, TA.)

definition: A saddle for a camel;
sourceDefinition: A saddle for a camel; (S, * K;) as also ↓ raAHuwlN ; (O, L, K;) for a he-camel and a she-camel; (TA;) the thing for the camel that is like the saroj for the horse or similar beast; (Mgh;) the thing that is put upon the camel for the purpose of riding thereon; (Er-Rághib, TA;) smaller than the qatab ; (S, TA;) one of the vehicles of men, exclusively of women: (TA:) [this seems to be regarded as the primary signification by the authors of the Mgh and the K and by Er-Rághib: but see what follows:] or it signifies the camel's saddle together with his [ girths called ] rabaD and Haqab and his [ cloth called ] Hilos [ that is put beneath the saddle ], and all its other appertenances: and is applied also to the pieces of wood of the raHol , without any apparatus: (AO, Sh, TA:) or it signifies anything, or everything, that a man prepares for removing, or journeying; such as a bag, or receptacle, for goods or utensils or apparatus, and a camel's saddle, and a [ cloth such as is called ] Hilos [ that is put beneath the saddle ], and a rasan [or rope for leading his camel ]: (Msb:) or it signifies as first explained above, and also the goods, or utensils, or apparatus, which a man takes with him [ during a journey ]: (S, K, TA:) [but accord. to the Msb, this signification is from another, mentioned below; and the same seems to be indicated in the S, which reverses the order in which I have mentioned the three significations that I quote from it:] this last signification is disapproved by El-Hareeree, in the “ Durrat el-Ghowwás: ” [but see two exs. voce Hu*aAfapN :] the pl. is A^aroHulN and riHaAlN ; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) the former a pl. of pauc.; (S, TA;) the latter, of mult. (TA.) One says, HaT~a raHolahu and A^aloqaY raHolahu [ He put down his camel's saddle ]; meaning he stayed, or abode. (TA.) And h`*aA maHaT~u Alr~iHaAli [ This is the place where the camels' saddles are put down ]. (TA.) And in reviling, one says, yaA A@bona muloqaYA^aroHuli Alr~ukobaAni [ O son of the place in which are thrown down the camels' saddles of the riders; as though the person thus addressed were there begotten]; (S, O, TA;) meaning yaA A@bona AlfaAjirapi [ O son of the adulteress or fornicatress ]: (TA in art. lqY :) or huwa Abn mlqY ArHl AlrkbAn [ He is the son &c.]. (Msb.) ― -b2- Er-Rághib, after giving the explanation mentioned as on his authority above, says that it is then sometimes applied to The camel [itself]: and is sometimes used in the sense next following; i. e. ― -b3- A part, of a place of alighting or abode, upon which on sits: (TA:) or a man's dwelling, or habitation; (S, K, TA;) [in the first of which, this commences the art., app. showing that the author held this to be the primary signification;]) his house or tent; and his place of alighting or abode: (TA:) a place to which a man betakes himself, or repairs, for lodging, covert, or refuge; a man's place of resort; (Mgh, Msb;) in a region, district, or tract, of cities, towns, or villages, and of cultivated land: and then applied to the goods, utensils, or apparatus, of a traveller; because they are, in travelling, the things to which he betakes himself: (Msb:) pl. A^aroHulN (TA) and riHaAlN [as above]. (Mgh, TA.) One says, daxalotu EalaY Alr~ajuli raHolahu , i. e. [ I went in to the man in ] his dwelling, or place of abode. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., A_i*aA A@botal~ati Aln~iEaAlu faSal~uwA fiY Alr~iHaAli , (TA,) or fiYlS~alaApu fiY Alr~iHaAli , (Mgh, and so in the TA in art. nEl ,) i. e. [ When the niEaAl are moistened by rain, then pray ye, or then prayer shall be performed,] in the houses, or habitations, or places of abode; the nEAl meaning here the HiraAr ; (IAth, TA in the present art.;) or rugged and hard tracts of ground; which are here particularized because the least wet moistens them, whereas the soft tracts dry up the water: (IAth, TA in art. nEl :) Az says that the meaning is, when the hard grounds are rained upon, they become slippery to him who walks upon them; therefore pray ye in your abodes, and there shall not be anything brought against you for your not being present at the prayer in the mosques of the congregations: (TA in that art.:) or the trad. may mean, then pray ye [ on the camels' saddles, i. e.] riding. (TA in the present art.) ― -b4- In another trad., it is related that 'Omar said to the Prophet, Haw~alotu raHoliYa AlbaAriHapa ; by the word raHol , as signifying [properly] either the “ place of abode and resort ” or the “ saddle upon which camels are ridden, ” alluding to his wife; meaning gi$oyaAnuhaA fiY qubulihaA mino jihapi ZahorihaA (TA.) ― -b5- raHolu AlmuSoHafi means The thing [or desk ] upon which the mSHf [or copy of the Kur-án ] is put, in shape [ somewhat ] like the saddle. (TA.) [It is generally a small desk of which the front and back have the form of the letter X; commonly made of palm-sticks.] -A2- [The pl.] raHaAlN also signifies [ Carpets, or cloths, or the like, such as are called ] TanaAfis , of the fabric of El-Heereh. (S, K.)
