definition: , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) aor. yaguwluhu , (Msb, TA,) inf. n. gawolN , (Mgh, Msb, TA,) He, or it, [accord. to the TA said of a thing,] destroyed him; (Lth, Mgh, Msb, K;) as also ↓ AgtAlhu : (K:) and (K) it (a thing, S, O) took him, seized him, or took him away, unexpectedly, at unawares, or from an unknown quarter; (S, O, K;) and so ↓ AgtAlhu : (S: [see also an ex. of this latter voce xaruwjN :]) and accord. to IAar, gAl Al$~aYo'u zayodFA signifies The thing took away Zeyd. (TA.) One says, ↓ gaAlatohu guwlN A [ cause of ] destruction destroyed him: (K, TA:) or [ destroyed him so that it was not known whither he had gone away; for] it is said of one who has fallen into destruction (S, TA) and it is not known whither he has gone away: (TA:) and it also signifies Death or the decree of death [ destroyed him, or took him away ]. (TA.) One says also when persons have perished in a land, gaAlatohumo tiloka AlA^aroDu [ That land caused them, or has caused them, to perish in it ]: and AlA^aroDu bifulaAnK ↓ tagaw~alati means The land caused such a one to perish; and to pursue a course that led him astray. (TA.) And one says of a land ( A^aroD ), taguwlu Als~aAbilapa , meaning It casts away the travellers, or wayfarers; causes them to fall, or drop down; and removes them far away. (TA.) ― -b2- gaAlati Alxamoru fulaAnFA means (assumed tropical:) The wine that he had drunk deprived such a one of his reason: or, of the soundness of his body: (AHeyth, TA:) [or corrupted, or vitiated, him; for] gaAlahu , aor. yaguwluhu , signifies A^afosadahu ; (Ksh and Bd in xxxvii. 46;) as well as A^aholakahu : (Ksh, ibid:) and a poet, cited by AO, says, wamaA zaAlati AlkaA^osu tagotaAlunaA (assumed tropical:) [ And the cup of wine caused not to deprive us of our reason ]. (S, O.) ― -b3- taguwlu Alv~iyaAba fataqoSuru EanohaA is said of a tall woman [app. as meaning She exceeds the measure of the clothes, so that they are too short for her ]: such a woman is said to be ↓ *aAtu gawolK . (TA.) ― -b4- And one says, maA gaAlaka Ean~aA i. e. What withheld, or debarred, or has withheld or debarred, thee from us? (O.) ― -b5- And gulotuhu , inf. n. giyaAlapN and giyaAlN and guw^uwlN , signifies I stole it. (O and TA in art. gyl [though belonging to art. gwl ].)

sourceDefinition: is syn. with mubaAdarapN [The hastening, making haste, or striving to be first or beforehand, in doing or attaining or obtaining a thing], (S, O, K, TA,) [or] in journeying, &c. (TA.) Jereer says, (S, O,) or El-Akhtal, (so in the TA,) mentioning a man upon whom horsemen had made a sudden attack, (S, TA,) EaAyanotu mu$oEilapa AlriEaAli kaA^an~ahaA TayorN tugaAwilu fiY $amaAmK wukuwraA [ I saw those that were spreading themselves of the small parties of horsemen, as though they were birds hastening to nests in (the mountain of) Shemám ]. (S, O, TA.) And it is related in a trad. of 'Ammár, that he was brief in prayer, and said, kunotu A^ugaAwilu HaAjapF liY [ I was hastening to accomplish a want that I had ]. (TA.) And in a trad. of Keys Ibn-'Ásim, [it is related that he said,] kunotu A^ugaAwiluhumo fiY AljaAhiliy~api i. e. I used to strive to be beforehand with them ( A^ubaAdiruhumo ) in making a sudden attack or incursion, and in doing mischief, [ in the Time of Ignorance: ] or, as some relate it, it is with r [i. e. kunotu A^ugaAwiruhumo I used to make sudden attacks or incursions upon them ]. (TA.)

definition: Far extent of a desert, or waterless desert;
sourceDefinition: Far extent of a desert, or waterless desert; (S, O, TA;) because it destroys him who passes along in it: (S, TA:) or of a land; because it casts away the travellers, or wayfarers, causes them to fall, or drop down, and removes them far away: and accord. to Lh, it is said of a land when one journeys in it without stopping. (TA.) One says, maA A^aboEada gawola h`*ihi AlA^aroDi How far is the extent of this land! and A_in~ahaA labaEiydapu Algawoli [ Verily it is far in extent ]. (ISh, TA.) And A^aroDN *aAtu gawolK A land far extending, though in the view of the eye of little extent: (IKh, TA:) and gay~ilN applied to land is said to have the same meaning. (TA in art. gyl .) And A^agowaAlu AlA^aroDi [in which AgwAl is app. pl. of gawolN ] signifies The extremities of the land. (TA.) ― -b2- AimoraA^apN *aAtu gawolK A tall woman. (TA.) See 1, last sentence but two. [And see also gay~ilapN , voce gay~ilN , in art. gyl .] ― -b3- [ nAqp gwl AlnjA=' is a phrase mentioned without any indication of the meaning in the TA: perhaps naAqapu gawoli Aln~ajaA='i , and signifying A she-camel of an exceeding degree of swiftness. ] -A2- In the saying in the Kur [xxxvii. 46], laA fiyhaA gawolN , [referring to the wine of Paradise,] it means The evil result of headache; because it is said in another place, [lvi. 19,] laA yuSad~aEuwna EanohaA : (S, O, TA:) or it [there] means [simply] headache: or intoxication: (K, TA:) thus some expl. it as used in that instance: (TA:) or, as expl. by AO, it there means privation of the intellectual faculties. (S, O, TA.) ― -b2- See also guwlN , latter half. ― -b3- Also Distress, trouble, or molestation: (K, TA:) thus expl. by some as used in the Kur ubi suprà. (TA.) ― -b4- And Unfaithfulness; or unfaithful acting. (TA.) ― -b5- ↓ A^ataY gawolFA gaAy^ilapF means He did a cunning, bad, action. (K.) -A3- Also Much earth. (S, O, K.) Hence the phrase gawolFA mina Alr~amoli , [app. meaning A large quantity of sand, ] in a verse of Lebeed. (S, O.) ― -b2- And A collection of [ the trees called ] TaloH , (K, TA,) with which nothing participates. (TA.) ― -b3- And A low, or depressed, part of the earth, or of land. (K.)

definition: A kind of [ goblin, ] demon, devil, or jinnee, which, the Arabs assert, appears to men in the desert, assuming various forms, causing them to wander from the way, and destroying them;
sourceDefinition: A kind of [ goblin, ] demon, devil, or jinnee, which, the Arabs assert, appears to men in the desert, assuming various forms, causing them to wander from the way, and destroying them; (JM, and TA * on the authority of IAth;) but this the Prophet denied, saying, laA guwla ; by which, however, accord. to some, he did not mean to deny the existence of the gwl , but only the assertion of the Arabs respecting its assuming various forms and its being able to cause any one to go astray: (IAth, JM, * TA:) i. q. siEolaApN [q. v.]: or a sort of siEolaAp : (S, O, Msb:) or a male jinnee; the female being called siEolaAp : (Abu-l-Wefee ElAarábee, TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^agowaAlN and [of mult.] giylaAnN (S, O, Msb, K) and giwalapN : (O, TA:) and it signifies also an enchantress of the jinn: (K:) and a demon, or devil, that eats men: (En-Nadr, O, K:) or any jinnee, or devil, or animal of prey, that destroys a man: (TA:) or a certain beast, (K, TA,) terrible [ in appearance ], having tusks, or fangs, (TA,) seen by the Arabs, and known by them; and killed by Taäbbata Sharrà: (K, TA:) and such as varies in form or appearance, of the enchanters and of the jinn; (K, TA;) on his doing which, as is said in a trad., one should hastily utter the call to prayer, to prevent his mischief by the mention of God: (TA:) or anything by reason of which the intellect departs; as also ↓ gawolN : (K:) and anything that takes a man unexpectedly and destroys him: (S, O, Msb:) [whence] one says, AlgaDabu guwlu AlHilomi Anger [ is that which ] destroys, and does away with, forbearance, or clemency. (S, O.) ― -b2- Also Destruction: [or a cause thereof: ] and death; or the decree of death. (K.) See 1, second sentence. ― -b3- And A calamity, or misfortune; (K, TA;) as also ↓ gaAy^ilapN ; (TA;) of which latter the pl. in this sense is gawaAy^ilu ; (K, * TA;) thus mentioned by Ks. (Msb.) ― -b4- And A serpent: pl. A^agowaAlN : (K:) accord. to Az, the Arabs call serpents A^agowaAl ; and thus this word is said to mean in the verse of Imra-el-Keys, liyaqotulaniY waAlma$orafiY~u muDaAjiEiY wamasonuwnapN zuroqN kaA^anoyaAbi A^agowaAli [ To slay me, while the Meshrefee sword was my bedfellow, and so were sharpened, polished arrowheads, like the fangs of serpents ]: (O, TA: *) but AHát says that this is meant as an exaggeration: (TA:) and it is said that the poet here means devils. (O, TA.)

definition: [primarily] An instrument with which a thing is destroyed.
sourceDefinition: [primarily] An instrument with which a thing is destroyed. (Ham p. 648.) ― -b2- And [hence] used as meaning A knife: and in common acceptation, a knife that is put in the midst of a whip which is as a sheath to it: (Ham ibid.:) a knife to which a whip is a sheath: (Mgh:) or a slender sword, having a flat back ( lahu qafFA ), (S, O, Msb,) like the knife, (Msb,) the sheath of which is like the whip: (S, O:) or an iron [ weapon ] that is put within a whip, which thus becomes to it a sheath: (K:) or a whip in the interior of which is a sword: (A'Obeyd, TA:) said to be thus called because its owner destroys with it his enemy unexpectedly: pl. magaAwilu : (TA:) and a thing like a mi$omal [or short and slender sword over which a man covers himself with his garment ], except that it is more slender, and longer: (K:) and a long naSol [or blade ], (AHn, K, TA,) of little breadth, thick in the maton [which generally means the part in the middle of which is the ridge, but may here mean the back ]: (AHn, TA:) or a short sword which a man wears inwrapped beneath his clothes: (TA:) or a slender sword, having a flat back ( lahu qafFA ): (K:) or a slender iron [ weapon ], having a sharp edge and a flat back ( waqafFA ), which the assassin binds upon his waist in order that he may therewith destroy men. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] farasN *aAtu migowalK (tropical:) A mare having a quality, or faculty, of outstripping: (O, K, TA:) as though she destroyed the [other] horses so that they fell short of reaching her. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. firaArF (T, S, M, K, &c.) and farN (M, K) and mafarN (S, M, K) and mafirN , (K,) or the last is a n. of place [and of time], (S, M,) He (a man, T) fled: (T, S:) or he turned away or aside, to elude, and fled, (M, K, TA,) from a thing that he feared. (TA.) A^ayona A@lomafar~u [in the Kur lxxv. 10] means Whither is the [ fleeing or] turning away &c.? (M, TA:) or it may mean when is the time thereof? (TA:) and Ayn Almafir~u , another reading, where is the place of fleeing &c.? (I'Ab, Zj, S, M, TA,) as also Almifar~u , (Zj, K, TA,) which is an instrumental noun used as a noun of place: (K, TA:) but the first is the common reading. (TA.) ― -b2- far~a mino Eaduwihi , aor. as above, inf. n. far~N , He wheeled about widely from his enemy, to turn again. (Msb.) ― -b3- And far~a A_ilaY Al$~aYo'i He went, or betook himself, to the thing. (Msb.) ― -b4- And [hence] far~ato yaduhu His arm, or hand, fell off; like Tar~ato and tar~ato . (O.) -A2- far~a Alfarasa , (S, O,) or Ald~aAb~apa , (M, K,) aor. , (S, M, O,) i. e. with damm, (O,) [in copies of the K , but afterwards in those copies , which is the regular and correct form,] inf. n. far~N (S, M, O, K) and furaArN and firaArN and faraArN , (K,) or furaArN is a simple subst., and firaArN is an inf. n., (Meyd, in explanation of the prov. which here follows,) He looked at, or examined, the teeth of the horse, (S, O,) or he exposed to view the teeth of the beast that he might see what was its age. (M, K.) Hence, (TA,) A_in~a AljawaAda Eayonuhu furaAruhu (S, M, * Meyd, K, *) and firaAruhu , (M, Meyd, K,) and faraAruhu , (S, K,) sometimes thus pronounced with fet-h, (S,) (tropical:) [ Verily the fleet and excellent horse, his aspect (see EayonN ) is ( equivalent to ) the examination of his teeth, i. e. he is known by his aspect], is a prov., applied to him whose external state indicates his internal qualities; (Meyd, O, K;) meaning that one knows his excellence from his Eayon [i. e. aspect] like as one knows the age of a beast by examining his teeth; (TA;) his external appearance rendering it needless for thee to test him, (S, Meyd, O, K,) and to examine ( A^ano tafur~a ) his teeth: (S, O, K:) and [with the same meaning] one says, far~u AljawaAdi Eayonuhu : (A, TA:) and [in like manner] Alxabiyvu Eaynuhu furiAaruhu [ The bad, his aspect &c.]; (Meyd, O, TA;) i. e. thou knowest his badness by his Eayon when thou seest him. (TA.) And one says also, fararotu fama Alfarasi I opened the mouth of the horse that I might know his age. (Har p. 28.) And far~a Eano A^asonaAni Ald~aAb~api , aor. , He examined the teeth of the beast. (Har p. 233.) ― -b2- [Hence the saying of El-Hajjáj, furirotu Eano *akaA='K , expl. in art. *kw .] And [hence also] one says, far~ahu Eano A^a$oyaA='i (tropical:) He examined him respecting things (O, * TA.) And far~a AlA^amora , (M, TA,) and far~a Eani AlA^amori , (S, M, O, K, TA,) (tropical:) He examined, looked into, scrutinized, or investigated, the affair; searched into it; inquired, or sought information, respecting it. (S, M, O, K, TA.) And far~a fulaAnN Eam~aA fiY nafosiY (tropical:) Such a one interrogated me in order that he might know, from what I should say, what was in my mind. (TA.) ― -b3- And fur~a AlA^amoru ja*aEFA (assumed tropical:) The thing returned to its first state; it recommenced. (M, O, K.) And fur~a AlA^amora ja*aEFA (assumed tropical:) Commence thou the affair from the first thereof. (M, in the TT. [But the MS. has in this case, as in that here immediately preceding, AlAmru : the right reading is evidently AlAmra ; as in a similar phrase voce ja*aEN , q. v.]) -A3- far~a , aor. yafir~u or yafar~u , (accord. to different copies of the T,) He became intelligent after being weak [ in mind ]. definition: He, or it, made him to flee;

sourceDefinition: He laughed in a beautiful manner, (M, K,) beyond what is termed AinokilaAl [inf. n. of Ainokal~a , q. v.]. (M.) One says, Aftr~a DaAHikFA He showed his teeth laughing; (S;) as also Aftr Eano vagorihi . (T.) It is said of the Prophet, AlgamaAmi wa yafotar~u Eano mivoli Hab~i meaning And he used to smile so as to show teeth the like of hail-stones, without a reiterated, or a loud, laughing. (T.) ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) Aftr~ Albaroqu (assumed tropical:) The lightning glistened. (M, K.) sourceDefinition: , (S, M, K, &c.,) inf. n. farofaArN , (M,) or firofaArN , (TA,) He put in a state of motion, commotion, or agitation; shook; or shook about; (S, M, K;) it, (S, K,) or him. (M.) One says of a horse, yufarofiru All~ijaAma fiY fiyhi He puts in a state of motion, &c., the bit in his mouth. (M. [See also an explanation of the verb as intrans., in what follows.]) ― -b2- He broke it, i. e. a thing. (M, K.) ― -b3- He cut it. (K.) ― -b4- He clave, split, slit, rent, or tore, it. (TA.) [Thus] farofara signifies He rent, or tore, [skins such as are termed] ziqaAq [pl. of ziq~N ], and other things; (O, K, TA;) and slit, or rent, them much. (TA. [In two copies of the T, instead of Alz~iqaAqa wagayorahaA , the reading in the O and K and TA, I find AlruqAqa wgyrh .]) ― -b5- [ He mangled it. ] One says, Al*~iy^obu yufarofiru Al$~aApa The wolf mangles the sheep, or goat. (O, * TA.) ― -b6- And, (O, K, TA,) hence, (O,) inf. n. farofarapN , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) He defamed him, and mangled his reputation. (O, K, TA.) ― -b7- And (assumed tropical:) He discommended it, [ as though ] mangling it with discommendation: the verb occurs in this sense in a trad., having for its object Ald~unoyaA [meaning the enjoyments, or good, of the present world ]. (TA.) ― -b8- Also, (inf. n. farofarapN , TA,) He called or cried, or called out or cried out, to him. (M, K.) -A2- farofara as intrans., He (a camel) put his body in a state of commotion, or agitation. (M, K.) ― -b2- He (a horse) struck his teeth with the fA^os [q. v.] of his bit, and moved about his head. (S, O, K.) ― -b3- He hastened, or sped, and went with short steps. (M, O, K.) ― -b4- He was light, and unsteady, (S, * M, * O, * K, TA,) in mind; (TA;) inf. n. farofarapN . (S, M, O, TA.) ― -b5- He hastened, or was hasty, with foolishness, or stupidity. (IAar, T, TA.) ― -b6- And He confounded, or confused, and was profuse, fiY kalaAmihi [ in his speaking, or talking, or his speech, or talk ]. (M, K.) ― -b7- And [app. He talked; for] AlfarofarapN signifies AlkalaAmu [which is often used as a quasi-inf. n. of kl~m ]. (M.) -A3- farofara also signifies He made the kind of vehicle called farofaAr . (T, K.) ― -b2- And He kindled [a fire] with [ wood of ] the species of tree called farfaAr . (T, K.)

(O.) [See also a similar prov. in art. sfh , conj. 5.]

sourceDefinition: , (S in this art. and in art. fln , and K and TA in the latter art.,) meaning yaA fulaAnu [ O such a one ], (S &c.,) with refa and without tenween, (TA,) is sometimes said to one person, [i. e. to a man,] and yaA fulaAni to two persons, and yaA fuluwna to a pl. number; and yaA fulapu to a female, and yaA fulataAni to two females, and yaA fulaAtu to a pl. number of females, (K, TA,) and sometimes yaA fulaApu , (K, * TA,) thus correctly, of the dial. of some of the tribe of Temeem, in the copies of the K erroneously written yA fulaAtu , (TA,) is said, and some say yaA fula , [in the CK yAflu , but correctly yAfula , i. e., as is said in the TA, binaSobi All~aAmi ,] meaning yaA fulapu : (K, TA:) [J says,] yaA fulu , without teshdeed, said in calling to a person, is apocopated from yaA fulaAnu ; not formed in the way of taroxiym , for if it were an instance of trxym they would say yaA fulaA : (S in this art.:) [or,] accord. to Sb, yaA fulu is not held to be an instance of a word from which is elided something that is retained when it is not [thus] used in calling to a person, but the noun in this case is made to be of two letters in the manner of damN [which is originally damawN or damFY or damoYN ], and it is thus made to be of two letters because a word that is used in calling to a person or thing is a subject for elision: (M in this art.:) and sometimes ful was used otherwise than in calling to a person, by poetic license, as in the saying of Abu-n-Nejm, fiY laj~apK A^amosiko fulaAnFA Eano fuli (S and M in this art.,) meaning En fulaAnK [i. e. In, or amid, a multitude of cries, or noises: (thus expl. in the S:) withhold thou such a one from such a one ]: (S in art. fln :) and Sb disallowed the saying fulu as meaning fulaAn [in the CK (erroneously) yA fulu as meaning yA fulaAnu ] except [in the vocative form of speech and] in poetry: (M and K and TA in art. fln :) [but] they said [also] fulu bonu fuli , [said to be] an instance of an elision, (T and M in art. fln ,) i. e. of the elision of a final w [accord. to some, who hold fulaAnN to be originally fulowaAnN ]; (T;) like as they said haY~u bonu baY~K : (T, M:) and A^aYo fulo , with the l quiescent, occurs in a trad. respecting the resurrection; meaning yaA fulaAnu : (TA:) Ibn-Buzurj says that some of the tribe of Asd [i. e. Pepper; ] a sort of berry, ( Hab~N , S, O, K,) brought from India, (O, K, *) well known, (S, M, O,) not growing in the land of the Arabs, but often mentioned in their language: AHn was informed by one who had seen it that its tree is just like the pomegranate; (M, TA;) but Dáwood the hakeem adds that it is taller; (TA;) between the pair of leaves thereof are two fruit-stalks, regularly disposed, each fruitstalk of the length of the finger; and it is green, and is then plucked, and spread in the shade, and becomes black and shrivelled; and it [ the tree ] has thorns, like those of the pomegranate: when it [i. e. the fruit ] is fresh and moist, it is preserved with water and salt until it becomes mature, when it is eaten like as preserved herbs are eaten upon the tables of food, and it is a digestive: the n. un. is ↓ fulofulapN [app. meaning a peppercorn, like Hab~apu fulofulK : and Hab~u fulofulK means peppercorns, collectively]: (M, TA:) Dáwood says, in the “ Tedhkireh, ” that its leaves are thin, red next the tree and green in the other direction, and its wood is lank and soft: and it is white and black: (TA:) the white is the better. (TA.) [A long description of its properties, with additions in the TA, some of them well known and others fanciful, I omit as being needless.] ― -b2- daArufuloful , or ↓ daArufilofil , (accord. to different copies of the K,) [app. daArufulofulN , or perhaps daArafulofulN , a compound of two words (both originally Pers.) made one, as such written in the K with the article ( Ald~Arflfl ), and perfectly declinable, because (although a compound of two nouns) it is not a proper name,] is The tree of the fuloful when it first bears fruit, accord. to the K; but several writers declare that the tree of [the] dAr flfl is not the same as the tree of the flfl : (MF, TA:) [ dAr flfl is one of the names now applied to long pepper, and is commonly pronounced daArofilofilo :] it is [generally] known in Egypt by the name of Eiroqu Al*~ahabi , [another term, now used, for long pepper,] and is called in Pers. PlPl drAz [i. e. PuloPildaraAz , the latter of which words signifies “ long ”]: (TA:) it increases the venereal faculty, causes the food to digest; removes colic, (K, TA,) and flatulence; (TA;) and is beneficial as a remedy against the bite, or sting, of venomous reptiles, applied as a liniment, with oil. (K, TA.) ― -b3- fulofulN is also a name sometimes applied to The fruit of the barowaq [q. v., in art. brq ]; likening it to the fulofulN mentioned before [i. e. to peppercorns]: he who pronounces it, when thus applied, ↓ filofilN errs; for this signifies the fruit of certain trees of the [ kind called ] EiDaAh ; and the people of El-Yemen call thus [particularly] the fruit of the [ species of EiDaAh . termed ] gaAf [q. v.]. (M.) ― -b4- fulofulu AlmaA='i is the name of A certain plant growing in the neighbourhood of water, lank, soft, or smooth, in the leaves, having berries ( Hab~i ) in bunches. (TA.) ― -b5- fulofulu Alquruwdi is The same as Hb~ Allym [but what this is I do not find]. (TA.) ― -b6- fulofulu AlS~aqaAlibapi is What is called [ in Pers. ] fnjnk$t [i. e. fanojanoku$ot : see Alfaqodu ]. (TA.) ― -b7- [ falaAfilu is pl. of fulofulN .] And falaAfilu Als~uwdaAni is the name of Certain berries ( Hab~ ), round and smooth, in sheaths, or cases, ( guluf ,) and in receptacles ( A^aboyaAt ) like the Sanawobar [or cone of the pine, app. in form ]. (TA.) -A2- See also faliylN , last sentence. -A3- fulofulN signifies also A sharp, or clever, servant; (T, O, K;) and ↓ filofilN is said to signify thus likewise by Mullà 'Alee, in his “ Námoos, ” and even more commonly: but this requires consideration. (MF, TA.)

definition: , (S, K,) inf. n. taqoriyTN , (TA,) He adorned the girl, or young woman with the [ ornament called ] quroT . (S, * K.) A rájiz says, addressing his wife, (S, TA,) who had asked him to adorn her with...
sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) inf. n. taqoriyTN , (TA,) He adorned the girl, or young woman with the [ ornament called ] quroT . (S, * K.) A rájiz says, addressing his wife, (S, TA,) who had asked him to adorn her with a pair of ornaments of the kind so called, (TA,) qar~aTaki A@ll~`hu EalaY AlEayonayoni EaqaAribFA suwdFA waA^aroqamayoni (assumed tropical:) [ May God suspend to thee, upon the two eyes, black scorpions, and two black and white serpents ]. (S, TA.) [See also another tropical usage of the verb voce $an~afa .] ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) qr~T Alfarasa (tropical:) He put, or threw, the bridle ( lijaAm ) upon the horse's head; (S, TA;) this is what is meant by the explanation A^alojamahaA in the K: (TA:) or he placed the horse's reins behind his ears, in putting the bridle on his head: (Sgh, K: *) or it has the former of the meanings explained above, and also signifies, he (the rider) stretched forth his hand so as to put it upon the back of the horse's head, upon the place where the Ei*aAr is tied, while the horse was running: (IDrd:) or he incited the horse to the most vehement running; (TA, and so in the CK, excepting that Alxayola is there put in this instance in the place of Alfrs ;) because, when his running is vehement, the rein is extended upon the ear, and so becomes like the quroT : accord. to the A, qr~T Alfarasa EinaAnahu means (tropical:) he slackened the horse's rein so that it fell upon, or against, the part behind the ear, the place of the quroT , in urging him to run. (TA.) ― -b3- And hence, (A,) qar~aTotu A_ilayohi rasuwlFA (tropical:) I hastened to him a messenger: (Ibn- 'Abbád, TA:) or I dismissed (lit. flung ) in haste to him a messenger: a phrase doubly tropical. (A, TA.) And hence taqoriyTN is used by the vulgar to signify the act of (tropical:) notifying: and (tropical:) desiring to hasten: and (tropical:) straitening: and (tropical:) confirming, or corroborating, in an affair or a command: in all which senses it is trebly tropical. (TA.) -A2- qr~T Ealayohi (tropical:) He gave him little; (K, TA;) or by little and little. (TA.) [This is said in the TA to be from AlqiraATu ; app. meaning from AlqiraATu as a dial. var. of AlqiyraATu : but IDrd says, that from this phrase is derived AlqyrAT .] -A3- [ He cut, or clipped, money.]

definition: [ An ear-ring, or ear-drop;
sourceDefinition: [ An ear-ring, or ear-drop; ] i. q. $anofN : (K:) or the thing that is suspended to the lobe of the ear; (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA;) such as a silver bead fashioned like a pearl, or a pendant of gold; the $nf being that which is in the upper part of the ear: (TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aqoriTapN (Mgh, Msb) and A^aqoraATN , (K,) and [of mult.] qiraTapN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and qiraATN (S, K) and quruwTN . (K.) It is said in a proverb, xu*ohu walawo biquroTaY maAriyapa [ Take thou it, although by means of giving for it the two earrings of Máriyeh ]; (TA, S, K, in art. mrY ;) i. e., take thou it at all events: (K in art. mrY :) this Máriyeh, respecting whom authors differ, was the first Arab woman who wore ear-rings, and her ear-rings are said to have been of great value. (TA.) ― -b2- AlquroTu (tropical:) The Pleiades ( Alv~uray~aA ): so called by way of comparison. (TA.) -A2- A certain plant, like the ruTubap [or raTobap , a species of trefoil, or clover ], except that it is superior in size, or quality, to the latter, (AHn, K,) and larger in the leaves, fed upon by horses and the like; (AHn, TA;) in Persian $abo*ar [or $abodar ]. (AHn, K.) [See birosiymN .]

definition: (S, Msb, K) and ↓ qirATN , (K, TA,) like kitaAbN , (TA,) or ↓ qir~aATN ;
sourceDefinition: (S, Msb, K) and ↓ qirATN , (K, TA,) like kitaAbN , (TA,) or ↓ qir~aATN ; (as in some copies of the K) which last is the original form, as is shown by its pl., qaraAriyTu , (S, Msb,) and by its dim., qurayoriyTN , (Msb,) the same change being made in this instance as is made in diynaArN ; (S, Msb;) in the ancient Greek language, [ κεράτιον ,] said to signify A grain of the xuronuwb [or carob-tree ]: (Msb:) [and hence, the weight thereof; a carat; i. e. four grains; ] the half of a daAniq , (S, Msb,) accord. to the ancient Greeks: (Msb voce dAnq , q. v.) or it is a weight differing in different countries; in Mekkeh being the twenty-fourth part of a deenár; and in El-'Irák, the twentieth part thereof: (K:) or the twentieth part of a deenár in most countries; but accord. to the people of Syria, the twenty-fourth part thereof. (IAth.) As occurring in a trad., (S, TA,) in which it is said, that he who attends a corpse until it is prayed over shall have a qiyraAT , and he who attends it until it is buried shall have qiyraATaAni , (TA,) qyrAT is explained as meaning, The like of Mount Ohod; (S, TA;) [i. e. a very great reward;] and qyrATAn as meaning the like of two great mountains. (TA.) ― -b2- qiyraATN is also applied by accountants to The twenty-fourth part of a thing; because twenty-four is the first number that has an eighth and a sixth and a fourth and a third and a half without a fraction. (Msb.)

definition: The covering of a thing, whether natural or accidental;
sourceDefinition: The covering of a thing, whether natural or accidental; (M, K;) i. e., of anything; (M;) [the exterior part, peel, rind, bark, coat, crust, integument, skin, or covering, of a branch, plant, fruit, or the like; a coat such as one of those of an onion or other bulbous root, as is shown in the K, voce muS~aAxN ; a case, husk, shale, shard, or shell, such as covers a seed or seeds or an egg; a crust, a scab, a substance consisting of scales or laminæ and any similar thing, that peels off from the skin &c.; the skin of fruits &c.;] of a branch [and the like], the part which is like the skin of a human being; and hence the qi$or of a melon and the like: (Msb:) pl. qu$uwrN . (S, M, Msb, K.) ↓ qi$orapN is a more particular term [signifying A piece, or particle, of peel, rind, bark, &c.]: (S:) and likewise signifies the skin of a haborap [or piece of flesh-meat] which remains when its liquor has been sucked; as also ↓ qu$orapN . (M.) ↓ qu$aArN also signifies the same as qi$orN : and likewise the skin [or slough ] of a serpent. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] qitorN also signifies (tropical:) The dress, or apparel, of a man; (S;) any dress, or apparel: (M, K:) and a garment; (TA;) as also ↓ qi$orapN : (M, TA:) and the pl. is qu$uwrN . (M, K.) You say, Ealayohi qi$orN HasanN (tropical:) [ Upon him is goodly apparel ]. And xaraja bayona qi$oratayoni naZiyfatayoni (tropical:) He went forth in two clean garments. (TA.) And in a trad. of Keyleh it is said, kunotu A_i*aA raA^ayotu rajulFA *aA ruwaA='K wa*aA qi$orK TamaHa baSariY A_ilayohi (tropical:) [ I used, when I saw a man of goodly aspect, and of apparel, to raise my eyes towards him ]. (S.) ― -b3- [Hence, also,] ↓ qu$aArN signifies (assumed tropical:) The refuse, or lowest or basest or meanest sort, of mankind, or of people. (IAar, in TA, arts. b$r and x$r .) See also qu$aArahN . ― -b4- And see qu$orN .

definition: [A $aj~ap (or wound upon the head) which merely peels off the external skin;
sourceDefinition: [A $aj~ap (or wound upon the head) which merely peels off the external skin; also termed HaAriSapN ; (see $aj~apN ;)] the first $aj~ap , (S, K,) because it peels off the skin, (S,) or which peels off the skin. (K.) ― -b2- A woman who peels her face, (K,) i. e., the external skin of her face, with medicine [ called qa$uwrN ], in order that her complexion may become clear; (K, TA;) and who rubs her face, or the face of another, with [ the kind of liniment called ] gumorap ; (TA;) as also ↓ maqo$uwrapN : (K:) which latter [also] signifies a woman to whom this is done. (TA.) The qaA$irap and the maqo$uwrapN are cursed in a trad. (M, K.) ― -b3- maTorapN qaA$irapN , (S,) and ↓ qu$orapN , and ↓ qu$arapN , (M, K, TA,) A rain that pares, or strips, the surface of the earth, (S, M, K, TA, [in the K, maTarN yaqo$iru is put in the place of maTorapN taqo$iru , in the M]) and removes the pebbles from the ground, being a rain that falls with vehemence. (TA.) ― -b4- sanapN qaA$irapN , (TA,) and ↓ qaA$uwrapN , (S, M, K,) and ↓ qaA$uwrN , (M, K,) (tropical:) A year that strips, or strips off, everything: (M, K:) or that strips, or strips off, men; and camels or the like: (M:) a year of sterility, drought, or dearth. (S.) See also A^aqo$aru .

definition: The thing, (S,) or wide piece of rag, (Msb,) with which a child is bound (S, Msb) in the cradle: (S:) or the piece of rag, (Mgh, K,) or wide piece of rag, (TA,) which is wound upon a child (M, K, TA) when he is bound in the cradle: (Mgh, TA: *) pl.
sourceDefinition: The thing, (S,) or wide piece of rag, (Msb,) with which a child is bound (S, Msb) in the cradle: (S:) or the piece of rag, (Mgh, K,) or wide piece of rag, (TA,) which is wound upon a child (M, K, TA) when he is bound in the cradle: (Mgh, TA: *) pl. qumuTN . (Mgh, Msb.) ― -b2- A rope with which the legs of a sheep or goat are bound (S, Mgh, K) on the occasion of the slaughtering; (S, K;) as also ↓ qimoTN : (K:) or a rope with which the arms and legs, or hands and feet, of a captive are bound together: (Msb, K:) pl. as above; (Mgh;) and the pl. of qumuTN [probably a mistranscription for qimoTN ] is A^aqomaATN . (TA.) ― -b3- qumuTN also signifies The $uruT , (Mgh, Msb,) meaning wide woven ropes, (Mgh,) of fibres or leaves of the palm-tree, by which a booth of reeds or canes is bound: or, as some say, the pieces of wood that are upon the outside of a booth of reeds or canes, or in its inside, to which are bound the bundles of reeds or canes that form the roof: (Mgh, Msb:) or the heads [or extremities ] thereof: (Msb:) or qmT , with damm, [app. meaning qumuTN , with damm to the second letter as well as the first, or qumoTN as a contraction of qumuTN , like as kutobN , accord. to some, is a contraction of kutubN ,] as IAth says, on the authority of Hr, (TA,) or ↓ qimoTN , with kesr, (S, K,) signifies the thing, (S,) or rope, (K, TA,) of fibres or leaves of the palmtree, (TA,) with which booths of reeds or canes are bound: (S, K, TA:) and hence maEaAqidu AlqimoTi [ the places where such ropes are tied ]. (S.) ― -b4- Also qimaATN (assumed tropical:) The snares by which one snares men: and [its pl.] qumuTN , accord. to the A, (tropical:) the cords of stratagems or tricks. (TA.) [Hence,] waqaEotu EalaY qimaATihi (assumed tropical:) I became acquainted with his stratagems, or tricks, (Lth, K,) or his snares by which he snares men. (TA.) [The explanation of this phrase by Lth is wqEt EalY bunuwdihi : that in the K, faTinotu bunuwdahu : another explanation is given in the TA, which is, faTinotu lahu fY tuw^adapK : in the JK, faTanotu bituw^awdapK : the right reading in the K and JK seems to be faTinotu bibunuwdihi : and that of the explanation in the TA mentioned in this sentence is most probably, I think, faTinotu lahu fiY bunuwdihi I understood him in his stratagems, &c.]

definition: One who takes, captures, catches, insnares, entraps, hunts, or chases, wild animals or the like;
sourceDefinition: One who takes, captures, catches, insnares, entraps, hunts, or chases, wild animals or the like; as also ↓ qaniySN (S, M, A, K) and ↓ qan~aASN : (S, M, K:) or ↓ qaniySN signifies persons who do so, collectively; and is [a quasi-pl. n.] similar to kaliybN and maEiyzN and HamiyrN : (IJ, TA:) the pl. of qaAniSN is qun~aASN : (A, TA:) and ↓ qaAniSapN signifies the same as the pl.: and also low, vile; or mean, persons. (TA. [See also TumoruwrN , in an explanation of which the sing. qaAniSN is app. used in like manner.]) You say, jaA='a AlqaniySu biAloqaniySi The sportsman came with the game taken. (A.) And it is said in a trad., fatuxoriju Aln~aAru Ealayohimo qawaAniSa (assumed tropical:) [ And the fire of hell shall send forth against them snatchers ]; meaning, it shall snatch them in pieces like as the beast or bird of prey snatches its prey: the sing. is ↓ qaAniSapN : (K, TA:) or, as some say, the meaning is, sparks like the qawaAniS of birds, i. e., their HawaASil . (TA.) See what follows.

(K.) And fulaAnN yaA^otiY bimaA yaA^otiY qayosFA (tropical:) [ Such a one does what he does, or says what he says, by measure, or by rule ]. And qaAsa Ealayohi He judged by comparison therewith. And He copied it as a model. ]

definition: Reaped grain collected together;

(S, A, Msb.)

definition: The stomach of a sucking kid became a kari$ : (S, K:) i.
sourceDefinition: The stomach of a sucking kid became a kari$ : (S, K:) i. e., when he pastured upon herbage; (K;) for it is called AnfHp as long as the kid does not eat; but when he eats, it is called kr$ . (S.) ― -b2- Also Astkr$ He (a kid, and a boy,) became large in his stomach: or became hard in his palate, and wide in his belly, after he had become large: (TA:) or he (a lamb or kid or calf) became large in his belly: (IAar:) or he (a lamb or kid) became large in his belly, and ate much: (TA:) or he (a kid, A, and a boy, Az, TA) became large in his belly, and began to eat: (Az, A, TA,) but some disapprove of its being said of a boy, asserting that one says of a boy A_isotajofara . (TA.) ― -b3- See also 2.

definition: and ↓ kiro$N [The stomach, or man, of any ruminant animal;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ kiro$N [The stomach, or man, of any ruminant animal; ] the part of any ruminant, (S, K,) or of the animal that has a xuf~ , [here meaning of the camel, ] and of such as has a divided hoof, (A, Msb,) that corresponds to the maEidap of a man: (S, A, Msb, K:) [it is in most cases four-fold; consisting of the first stomach, commonly called the paunch, which is the largest, and has no rugæ upon its internal surface, but a villous coat, having innumerable blunt papillæ which give it a general roughness, and from this the food is forced back into the mouth to be ruminated, as it is also from the second; the honeycomb stomach, which is the second, and which is so called from the cells which form its internal coat; the omasum, which is the third, and smallest, stomach, by some called the millet, but commonly the manyplies, because its internal surface has many plies, or folds, and strata super strata; and the abomasum, or fourth stomach, commonly called the rennetbag, or runnet bag, and the red, or reed, which is next in size to the paunch, and has an internal villous coat like that of the human stomach, but with longer and looser inner plies, or folds, and in this alone the true digestive process takes place:] but it is only thus called after the animal has begun to eat; being previously called A_inofaHapN : (S, TA:) [or, accord. to some, the term is applied to the first and second stomachs, together; for it is said that] it empties itself into the qaTinap [or third stomach ], as though it were yadu jiraAbK [so in my original, but this seems to be a mistranscription for lahu jiraAbN , meaning a provisionbag for the animal ]: and it also pertains to the have or rabbit, and the jerboa: and is used [tropically] for that of man (TA:) it is of the fem gender: (S, K:) pl. [of pane.] A^akoraA$N (TA) and [of mult.] kuruw$N . (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- Hence the saying, (S, TA,) A_ino wajadotu A_ilaY *`lika faA kari$K , [in the CK, erroneously, faAkori$o .] meaning, (tropical:) If I find to that a way; (S, K, * TA;) said by a man upon whom one has imposed a difficult task; and originating from the fact that a man divided a sheep, or goat, in pieces, and put them into its stomach to cook them; and it was said to him, “ Put in the head ” whereupon he replied in the above words. (S, TA.) You say also, maA wajadotu A_ilayohi faA kari$K (tropical:) I have not found to him, or it, a way. (TA.) And lawo wajadotu A_ilayohi faA kari$K , and baAba kari$K , and A^donaY fiY kari$K , meaning, (tropical:) Had I found to him, or it, as much way as the mouth of a stomach, and the entrance of a stomach, and the least mouth of a stomach, laA^atayotuhu [ I had come to him, or I had done it ]. (Lh, TA.) And it is said in a trad. of El-Hajjáj, lawo wajadotu A_ilaY damika faA kari$K la$aribati AlbaToHaA='u minoka , meaning, (tropical:) Had I found a way to [ shed ] thy blood [ the small pebbles of the bottom of the water-course had drunk from thee ]. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] you say, of land ( A^aroD ), A_igobar~ato jilodatuhaA waraq~ato kari$uhaA [lit. Its skin became dusty, and its stomach became thin ]; meaning, (tropical:) it became sterile. (TA.) -A2- And [hence,] (tropical:) A receptacle for perfumes, and for clothes: in this sense also fem.: and a place of collection of anything. (TA.) -A3- And (tropical:) A man's family, or household: and his young children: (A, K:) or his family, or household, consisting of his young children. (S, Msb.) You say, jaA='a yajur~u kari$ahu (tropical:) He came dragging along his family, or household. (A, TA.) And Ealayohi kari$N mino EiyaAlK (tropical:) Upon him is dependent a large family. (A, * TA, in art. bqr .) And humo , (S,) or lahu , (A,) kari$N manovuwrapN , (S, A,) (tropical:) They are, (S,) or he has, (A,) scattered young children. (S, A.) And tazaw~aja fulaAnapa fanavarato lahu kari$ahaA , (S, A, *) and baTonahaA , (S,) (tropical:) He married, or took to wife, such a woman, and she bore to him many children. (S, A.) [See also art. nvr .] ― -b2- Also, (tropical:) A company, or congregated body, (S, A, Msb, K,) of men: (S, A, Msb:) pl. A^akoraA$N . (A.) Hence the saying of Mohammad, AlA^anoSaAru kari$iY waEayobatiY (S, TA) (tropical:) The Ansár are my company, and my companions, whom I acquaint with my secrets, and in whom I trust, and upon whom I rely: (TA:) or the meaning is, they are my auxiliaries, from whom I derive aid; because the camel and the beast with a divided hoof draw the cud from the stomach: (TA:) or the depositories of my secrets and trusts, like as the kr$ is the place of the food of the beast: (A:) or the objects of my love and compassion like young children. (Msb.) [And hence, app.,] Alkari$aAni is an appellation applied to [the tribes of] ElAzd and 'Abd-el-Keys. (S.) ― -b3- Also, (tropical:) The main part, or body of a people or company of men: (A, TA:) pl. A^akoraA$N and kuruw$N : or, as some say, these are pls. having no sing. [in this sense.] (TA.) -A4- vawobu A^akoraA$K [app. from some peculiarity in its colours or texture,] (tropical:) A kind of garment, or cloth, of the description termed buruwd of [ the fabric of ] El-Yemen. (Az, TA.)

rawSourceText: and ↓ kiro$N [The stomach, or man, of any ruminant animal; ] the part of any ruminant, (S, K,) or of the animal that has a xuf~ , [here meaning of the camel, ] and of such as has a divided hoof, (A, Msb,) that corresponds to the maEidap of a man: (S, A, Msb, K:) [it is in most cases four-fold; consisting of the first stomach, commonly called the paunch, which is the largest, and has no rugæ upon its internal surface, but a villous coat, having innumerable blunt papillæ which give it a general roughness, and from this the food is forced back into the mouth to be ruminated, as it is also from the second; the honeycomb stomach, which is the second, and which is so called from the cells which form its internal coat; the omasum, which is the third, and smallest, stomach, by some called the millet, but commonly the manyplies, because its internal surface has many plies, or folds, and strata super strata; and the abomasum, or fourth stomach, commonly called the rennetbag, or runnet bag, and the red, or reed, which is next in size to the paunch, and has an internal villous coat like that of the human stomach, but with longer and looser inner plies, or folds, and in this alone the true digestive process takes place:] but it is only thus called after the animal has begun to eat; being previously called A_inofaHapN : (S, TA:) [or, accord. to some, the term is applied to the first and second stomachs, together; for it is said that] it empties itself into the qaTinap [or third stomach ], as though it were yadu jiraAbK [so in my original, but this seems to be a mistranscription for lahu jiraAbN , meaning a provisionbag for the animal ]: and it also pertains to the have or rabbit, and the jerboa: and is used [tropically] for that of man (TA:) it is of the fem gender: (S, K:) pl. [of pane.] A^akoraA$N (TA) and [of mult.] kuruw$N . (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- Hence the saying, (S, TA,) A_ino wajadotu A_ilaY *`lika faA kari$K , [in the CK, erroneously, faAkori$o .] meaning, (tropical:) If I find to that a way; (S, K, * TA;) said by a man upon whom one has imposed a difficult task; and originating from the fact that a man divided a sheep, or goat, in pieces, and put them into its stomach to cook them; and it was said to him, “ Put in the head ” whereupon he replied in the above words. (S, TA.) You say also, maA wajadotu A_ilayohi faA kari$K (tropical:) I have not found to him, or it, a way. (TA.) And lawo wajadotu A_ilayohi faA kari$K , and baAba kari$K , and A^donaY fiY kari$K , meaning, (tropical:) Had I found to him, or it, as much way as the mouth of a stomach, and the entrance of a stomach, and the least mouth of a stomach, laA^atayotuhu [ I had come to him, or I had done it ]. And it is said in a trad. of El-Hajjáj, lawo wajadotu A_ilaY damika faA kari$K la$aribati AlbaToHaA='u minoka , meaning, (tropical:) Had I found a way to [ shed ] thy blood [ the small pebbles of the bottom of the water-course had drunk from thee ]. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] you say, of land ( A^aroD ), A_igobar~ato jilodatuhaA waraq~ato kari$uhaA [lit. definition: [ A sort of haggess;
sourceDefinition: [ A sort of haggess; or man stuffed with flesh-meat, or flesh-meat and fat, and cooked; ] a piece of the stomach of a ruminant, stuffed with flesh-meat, and fastened together with a skewer, and cooked: (A:) or a sort of food, made of flesh-meat and fat, in a piece cut out from the stomach of a camel; (K;) a sort of food of the people of the desert, made by taking flesh-meat marbled with fat ( laHom A^a$omaT ), well cut up into small pieces, and putting with it fat cut up in like manner, then putting it into a piece cut out from the stomach of a camel, after it has been washed, and its smooth side which is without any villous substance or feces has been cleansed, and fastening its edges together with a skewer, and digging for it a hole for fire, of the size thereof, and throwing into it heated stones, and lighting a fire over them, so that they become of a red heat, like fire, when the coals are put aside from them, and the mkr~$h is buried therein, and hot ashes are put over it; then some thick and tough firewood is kindled over it, and it is left until it is thoroughly well cooked, whereupon it is taken out, having become like one piece, the fat having melted with the flesh, and it is eaten with dates, being sweet. (Az, TA.)

definition: Milk that is pure, sheer, free from admixture, unmingled, unmixed, or clear;
sourceDefinition: Milk that is pure, sheer, free from admixture, unmingled, unmixed, or clear; (Lth, S, A, K;) without froth; (Lth, A;) or not mixed with water: (S, Msb;) whether sweet or sour; no other milk being so called: (S:) but it occurs repeatedly in trads. as meaning milk absolutely: (TA:) pl. miHaADN . (K.) It is said in a trad. ( baAriko lahumo fiY maHoDihaA wamaxoDihaA Do Thou bless them in their [the beasts'] pure milk and churned milk. (TA.) And in another, faA@EomiduwA A_ilaY $aApK mumotaliy^apF $aHomFA wamaHoDFA [ And betake yourselves to a ewe, or she-goat, ] fat, and abounding with milk. (TA.) [See also an ex. voce zubodN : and another voce Sar~aHa .] ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) Anything (Az, TA) pure, sheer, free from admixture, unmingled, unmixed, genuine, or clear; (Msb, TA;) that is not mixed with any other thing. (Az, Msb, TA.) You say, fiD~apN maHoDN , (K,) and maHoDapN , (A, K,) and ↓ mamoHuwDapN , (K,) (tropical:) Pure, unmixed, unalloyed, silver: (A, * K:) so says Sb: but you say, h`*ihi AlfiD~apu maHoDFA (tropical:) [ This is silver in a pure state ]; putting the last word in the accus. case, used as an inf. n. (TA.) And EarabiY~N maHoDN (tropical:) An Arabian of pure, or unmixed, race, or lineage, or parentage: (S, A, Msb: *) [ a genuine Arabian: ] and the epithet is the same as fem. [and dual] and pl., (S, Msb,) accord. to the more approved usage; (Msb;) [for it is originally an inf. n.;] but you may, if you please, use the fem. and dual and pl. forms, as in the instances of [the synonymous epithets] qalobN and baHotN : (S:) and Aln~asabi ↓ huwa mamoHuwDu (tropical:) he is pure, or unmixed, in race, or lineage, or parentage: (K, TA:) and AlD~ariybapi ↓ mamoHuwDu (tropical:) rendered pure in nature, or disposition; (Az, O;) freed from faults or vices: (Az:) and maHoDu AlHasabi (tropical:) pure in grounds of pretension to respect: (TA:) and AlHasabi ↓ mamoHuwDu (tropical:) rendered pure therein: (O, K:) the pl. of maHoDN thus used is miHaADN [a pl. of mult.] and A^amoHaADN [a pl. of pauc.]. (TA.) You say also, A^uHib~uka Hub~FA maHoDFA (tropical:) [ I love thee with a pure, sincere, or true, love ]. (A.) And maHoDu AlA_iyomaAni occurs in a trad. as meaning (tropical:) Pure faith or belief. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, i. q. qat~N [ A kind of trefoil, or clover ]. (IKtt)

And maAra Als~inaAnu fiY AlmaToEuwni [ The spear-head moved from side to side in the person pierced ]. (A.) And AlT~aEonapu tamuwru The thrust inclines to the right and left. (TA.) And Aln~ujuwmu tamuwru The stars come and go. (TA.) And maAra AlgubaAru , inf. n. maworN , The dust moved to and fro: or became raised by the wind. (M, K.) ― -b2- It moved round about, (T, TA,) and to and fro: (TA:) it was in a state of commotion; in a state of tumult: (S, * M, Msb, K:) said of the sea, (Msb,) &c.: (M:) it was in a state of quick motion or commotion. (Msb.) It is said in a trad., that when the soul, or spirit, was blown into Adam, maAra fiY raA^osihi faEaTasa It circulated, and moved to and fro, in his head, and he sneezed. (TA.) And in the Kur, [lii. 9,] yawoma tamuwru Als~amaA='u maworFA On the day when the heaven shall actually be in a state of commotion, or tumult: so accord. to Ed-Dahhák: or shall move from side to side: so accord. to AO and Akh: (S:) or shall come and go; or move to and fro; or reel. (T.) And in a trad. of Ibn-Ez-Zubeyr, bikataAy^iba tamuwru karijoli AljaraAdi With troops moving to and fro, in a state of commotion, like the leg of the locust, by reason of their multitude. (TA.) You say also, maArati Aln~aAqapu fiY sayorihaA The she-camel was in a state of commotion, and reeled, in her pace, or going: and in like manner you say of a mare. (TA.) ― -b3- maA A^adoriY A^agaAra A^amo maAra , a saying of the Arabs, related by IAar, (TA,) I know not whether he have come to low country, or turned and returned to high country ( najod ): (S, TA:) or have come to the low country, or come to the high country. (IAar, K, * TA.) ― -b4- maAra Ald~amu (S, &c.) The blood ran, or flowed, upon the surface of the ground; (T, S, M, Msb, K;) and in like manner you say of tears, meaning they flowed: (M:) or the blood poured upon the surface of the ground, and went hither and thither, (TA,) sideways. (A.) ― -b5- See also 4.

sourceDefinition: , (T, S, A, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. naborN , (S,) He, (a man, S, A,) or it, (anything, T,) raised, or elevated, a thing: (T, S, A, K:) or naborN signifies specially the raising of the voice: (MF, from the first part of the Keshsháf:) or the rising of the voice; so with the Arabs; and one says nabara Alr~ajulu , inf. n. naborapN , meaning, the man spoke in a high tone: (IAmb:) and nabara , inf. n. naborapN , he (a man) uttered a sound: (A:) and [the inf. n.] naborapN , signifies the crying out, or shouting, from fright, or fear: (T, K:) and naborapu Almugan~iY , the singer's raising his voice from a low to a high pitch. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) and , (M, Msb, K,) inf. n. navorN (S, M, A, Msb, K) and nivaArN , (M, K,) or the latter is a simple subst., (S, A, Msb,) He scattered a thing, sprinkled it, strewed it, dispersed it, or threw it dispersedly, (Lth, T, M, A, Msb, K, TA,) with his hand; (Lth, T;) as, for instance, grain, (Lth, T,) and fruit and the like, (Msb,) walnuts and almonds and sugar, (Lth, T,) and pearls, &c.; (A;) as also ↓ nv~r , (M, K,) inf. n. tanoviyrN ; (TA;) [or the latter is with teshdeed to denote muchness, or frequency, or repetition, of the action; or its application to many objects: see manovuwrN .] ― -b2- navarati Aln~axolapu (tropical:) The palm-tree [ scattered or] shook off its unripe dates. (A.) ― -b3- wajaA^ahu fanavara A^amoEaA='ahu (tropical:) He smote him with a knife and scattered his intestines ]. (M, A.) ― -b4- laA^anovuran~aka navora Alkari$i (tropical:) [ I will assuredly scatter thine intestines like as one scatters the contents of the stomach of a ruminant beast ]: said in threatening. (A.) ― -b5- navara waladFA (tropical:) He (a man, M) had many children born to him. (M, K, TA.) And navarati AlmaroA^apu baTonahaA , (T, A, Mgh TA,) and *aA baTonihaA , (T, Mgh, TA,) and kari$ahaA , (A, in art. kr$ ,) (tropical:) The woman brought forth many children; (T, A, in art. kr$ ;) scattered children; llz~awoji to the husband. (Mgh.) ― -b6- natara AlkalaAma (tropical:) He spoke, or talked, much. (M, K, TA.) ― -b7- navara qiraA'atahu (tropical:) He hastened, or was quick, in his reading, or reciting. (A.) ― -b8- navara , aor. , inf. n. naviyrN , (tropical:) He (a beast of carriage, M, K, and a camel, M, and an ass, T) sneezed [app. so as to scatter the moisture in his nostrils ]: (T, M, K, TA:) or did with his nose what is like sneezing: (T:) he (an ass, and a sheep or goat) sneezed, and expelled what annoyed or hurt him, from his nose: (A:) or navarato she (a ewe or goat) ejected from her nose what annoyed or hurt her. (S.) And navara , (Fr, T, IAth, Mgh, Msb,) aor. , (T, IAth,) inf. n. navorN (T, Mgh) [and app. naviyrN , as above], (tropical:) He [a man] blew his nose; ejected the mucus from his nose; syn. AmotaxaTa ; (IAth;) as also ↓ Astnvr : (S, K, art. mxT :) and he ejected what was in his nose, of mucus, and of that which annoyed or hurt him, in performing the ablution termed wuDuwo' ; (Sgh, TA;) as also ↓ A^anovara , accord. to some: (TA:) or ↓ A^anovara signifies he ejected what was in his nose; or he emitted his breath from his nose; or he introduced the water into his nose; as also ↓ Antvr and ↓ Astnvr : (K:) but this last explanation is outweighed in authority; the form ↓ Anvr is disallowed by the leading lexicologists; and the author of the K, in respect of this form, follows Sgh, without due consideration: (TA:) [accord. to the more approved opinion,) navara signifies he scattered what was in his nose by the breath; as also ↓ Antvr and ↓ Astnvr : (S:) or, as some of the learned say, he snuffed up water, and then ejected what was in it, of anything annoying or hurting, or of mucus; as also ↓ Astnvr : (IAar, T, Mgh:) or ↓ Astnvr (T, M, IAth, K) and ↓ Antvr , (K,) he snuffed up water, and then ejected it (T, M, IAth, K) by the breath of the nose: (T, M, K:) accord. to some, navara and ↓ Astnvr signify he (a person performing wuDuwo' ) snuffed up water: but others say that the latter signifies he ejected what was in his nose, of mucus &c.; agreeably with a trad. to be cited below: (Msb:) IAar says, that ↓ Astnvr signifies he snuffed up water, and put in motion the navorap , or end of the nose, in purification: (T [in the Mgh, this explanation is ascribed to Fr:]) and Fr, that navara and ↓ Antvr and ↓ Astnvr signify he put in motion the navorap , in purification. (T.) It is said of Mohammad, kaAna yasotano$iqu valaAvFA fiY kul~i mar~apK yasotanoviru [ He used to snuff up water three times, every time ejecting it; &c.] and this indicates that ↓ Astnvr differs from Astn$q . (T, Mgh, Msb.) And it is said in a trad., A_i*aA A@sotano$aqota faA@novuro , (S, Msb,) and faA@noviro , with the conjunctive A , and with damm and kesr to the v , (Msb,) When thou snuffest up water, scatter what is in thy nose by the breath; (S;) or eject what is in thy nose, of mucus, &c.: (Msb:) or, as A'Obeyd relates it, ↓ faA^anoviro ; inf. n. A_inovaArN : (Msb:) or, as he relates it A_i*aA tawaD~aAta faA^anoviro , with the disjunctive A ; and he does not explain it; but the lexicologists do not allow ↓ A^anovara , from AlA_inovaAru ; one only says, navara and ↓ Antvr and ↓ Astnvr . (T.) No instance of ↓ Astnvr used transitively has been heard, except in a trad. of El-Hasan Ibn-'Alee, A^anofahu ↓ Aisotanovara [ He ejected the contents of his nose; or he blew his nose ]; as though the root [ navara ] were regarded in it, or as though it were made to import the meaning of naq~aY . (Mgh.)

definition: [ A single act of scattering, strewing, dispersing, or throwing dispersedly, with the hand.
sourceDefinition: [ A single act of scattering, strewing, dispersing, or throwing dispersedly, with the hand. And hence,] ― -b2- (tropical:) A sneeze: (K:) or the like thereof; peculiar to a beast of carriage (S) [or other beast, and a fish, as appears from what here follows.] It is said in a trad. (A, TA) of Kaab, (TA,) AljaraAdu navorapu HuwtK (A, TA) (tropical:) The locust is [produced by] the sneeze of a fish: or, as in a trad. of I'Ab, navorapu AlHuwti the sneeze of the fish. (TA.) [From this it is inferred that the locust is, like fish, lawful to be captured by one in a state of A_iHoraAm .] -A2- (tropical:) The end of the nose: (IAar, T:) or i. q., xayo$uwmN : (A:) or the xy$wm with what is next to it: (M, K:) and (M, A; but in the K, or) the interstice that is between the two mustaches, (S, M, A, K,) against the partition between the two nostrils: (S, M, K:) so [in a man and] in the lion: (S, M:) or the nose or the lion. (M.) ― -b2- Hence, (T, &c.,) Aln~avorapu , (T, S, M, K,) and navorapu AlA^asadi , (T, A,) (tropical:) Two stars, between which is the space of a span, ( $borN , [said in several law-books to be the twelfth part of a rumoH , and therefore twenty-two minutes and a half, accord. to modern usage; but there is reason to believe that ancient usage differed from the modern with respect to both these measures, and was not precise nor uniform;]) and in [or between ] which is a particle ( laToxN ) of white, as though it were a portion of cloud; it is the nose of Leo, [which the Arabs extended far beyond the limits which it has upon our globes, (see Al*~iraAEu ,)] (S, K,) and is a Mansion of the Moon: (S:) [app. the Aselli; Asellus Boreus and Asellus Australis; two small stars in Cancer, between which is a little cloud or nebula, called Præsepe: (see Pliny, l. xviii. c. 35:)] a certain star or asterism, which is of the stars or asterisms of Leo, and which is a Mansion of the Moon: (M:) [app. meaning the same, or Præsepe: ] or a certain star in the sky, as though it were a particle ( laTox ) of cloud, over against two small stars, in the science of astronomy pertaining to the sign of Cancer [ though accord. to the Arabs belonging to Leo ]: (T:) [app. Præsepe; the two small stars adjacent to it being the Aselli:] a certain star, as though it were a particle ( laToxN ) of cloud; so called because it appears as though the lion had ejected if from his nose: (A:) [app. meaning the same:] in the Megista [of Ptolemy] it is mentioned by the name of the manger [i. e., Præsepe ], and the name of the two small [for Almnyrp in my copy of Kzw, I read AlSfyrp ,] stars is the two asses [i. e., the Aselli]: (Kzw, Description of Cancer:) or the nose and nostrils of the lion, consisting of three obscure stars, near together: AlT~arofu is [ before them, and is ] the two eyes of the lion, consisting of two stars, before which is Aljabohapu , consisting of four stars: (AHeyth:) [app. meaning the Aselli together with Præsepe: ] three stars, near together; the nose of the lion; [app. meaning the same;] which compose the Eighth Mansion of the Moon: (Kzw, Description of the Mansions of the Moon:) [these descriptions apply to this Mansion of the Moon accord. to those who make Aln~awo' to signify “ the heliacal rising: ” see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl :] or the bright star [app. meaning b] in Cancer: (Kzw, Description of Cancer:) [this agrees with the place of the Eighth Mansion of the Moon accord. to those who make Aln~awo' to signify “ the anti-heliacal setting: ” see again manaAzilu Alqamar .] The Arabs say A_i*aA TalaEati Aln~avorapu qanaA^ati Albusorapu , meaning, When Alnvrp rises [heliacally], the unripe date begins to have its redness intermixed with blackness: its rising is very soon after that of Al$~iEoraY [or Sirius: about the epoch of the Flight, it rose heliacally, in central Arabia, on the 17th of July, O. S.; and Sirius, on the 13th of the same month]. (M.)

definition: What becomes scattered, strewn, or dispersed, of, or from, a thing;
sourceDefinition: What becomes scattered, strewn, or dispersed, of, or from, a thing; (S, Msb;) as also ↓ nuvaArapN , (M, K,) and ↓ navarN , (K, [but see munotavirN ,]) and, as some say, ↓ nivaArN : (Msb:) so the ↓ nuvaArap of wheat, and of barley, and the like: (Lh, M:) or nuvaArN signifies the crumbs of bread, and of everything, that become scattered around the table: (T:) or the crumbs of the table that become scattered around: as also ↓ nuvaArapN : (A:) or this last, what becomes scattered from the table, and is eaten in the hope of obtaining a recompense [ for preventing its being thrown away or trodden under foot ]. (Lh, M, K. *)

definition: , with kesr, a subst.
sourceDefinition: , with kesr, a subst. from navara , (S, A, Msb,) signifying The act of scattering, strewing, dispersing, or throwing dispersedly, [anything,] (Lth, T, A, Msb,) [and particularly fruits and the like, such as] walnuts and almonds and sugar [and money, &c., on festive occasions,] and grain. (Lth, T.) You say $ahidotu nivaAra fulaAnK I was present at, or I witnessed, such a one's scattering (Lth, T, A) of fruits, &c. (Lth, T.) And kun~aA fiY nivaArihi We were at his scattering. (A.) ― -b2- Also, What is scattered, strewn, dispersed, or thrown dispersedly, (A, Msb, TA,) of such things as sugar and fruits and the like, (A, TA,) [and money, &c., on festive occasions;] a subst., (A, TA,) in the sense of manovuwrN , (A, Msb, TA,) like kitaAbN in the sense of makotuwbN ; (Msb;) as also ↓ navarN . (A, TA.) [See also munotavarN .] You say A^aSanotu mina Aln~ivaAri I obtained [somewhat] of the scattered [sugar or fruits &c.]. (Msb.) And maA A^aSabonaA mino navari fulaAnK $ayoy^FA We did not obtain aught of such a one's scattered things, such as sugar and fruit. (TA.) ― -b3- Accord. to some, i. q. nuvaArN in the first of the senses explained above. (Msb.)

definition: , aor. and , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. na$ozN , (S, K,) or nu$uwzN , (Msb,) He rose, or raised himself, (S, A, Msb, K,) fiY AlmakaAni in the place, (S,) and fiY majolisihi in his sitting-place, (TA,) and...
sourceDefinition: , aor. and , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. na$ozN , (S, K,) or nu$uwzN , (Msb,) He rose, or raised himself, (S, A, Msb, K,) fiY AlmakaAni in the place, (S,) and fiY majolisihi in his sitting-place, (TA,) and Eano makaAnihi , (A,) or mino makaAnihi , (Msb,) from his place: (A, Msb:) or he rose a little in his sittingplace: (TA:) or he stood up after sitting. (TA.) Both forms of the aor. occur, accord. to different readings, (the former being the reading of the people of El-Hijáz, and the latter that of others, Fr, TA,) in the Kur, [lviii. 12,] waA_i*aA qiyla A@no$uizuwA faA@no$uizuwA , (Msb, TA,) meaning, accord. to Aboo-Is-hák, And when it is said, Rise ye and stand up, then do ye rise and stand up. (TA.) Accord. to IKtt, na$aza Alqawomu fiY majolisihimo signifies The people drew themselves together [ in their sitting-place to make room] for those sitting with them: and also they rose from their sitting-place, and stood up. (TA.) You say also, na$aza biAlqawomi fiY AlxuSuwmapi , inf. n. nu$uwzN , He rose with the people for the purpose of contention, altercation, or litigation. sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. nagaSN , (S,) He (a man, S,) failed of having his desire fully accomplished: (S, K:) but Lth says, that it is more commonly with teshdeed, i. e. ↓ nag~aSa , [unless this be a mistake for nug~iSa ,] inf. n. tanogiySN . (TA.) ― -b2- And in like manner, (S,) He (a camel) failed of having his full, or complete, draught, or drink. (S, K.) ― -b3- And It (beverage) was imperfect, or defective. (K.) ― -b4- See also 5. -A2- nagaSN (L, K) and nagoSN (L, TA) [both inf. ns., the verb of the former being app. nagiSa , used intransitively, and that of the latter nagaSa , used transitively, followed by A_ibilahu ,] also signify The bringing one's camels to the drinking-trough, and, when they have drunk, turning them back, and bringing others; (K;) taking forth, from every two camels, a strong camel, and putting in its place a weak camel; and thus as it were, making their drinking troublesome. (TA.) ― -b2- You say also, nagaSa Alr~ajulu Alr~ajula The man prevented the man from obtaining his share of water by interposing to hinder his camels from drinking: and in like manner, raEoyahu ↓ A^anogaSahu [ He prevented him from obtaining his share of pasturage for his camels ]: the verb in the latter instance being with A . (TA.) ― -b3- See also 2.

definition: , aor. , inf. n. naqobN , He perforated, pierced, bored, or made a hole through, or in, or into, anything: like vaqaba . (TA.) He made a hole through a wall. (S.) ― -b2- naqaba sur~apa Ald~aAb~api ,...
sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. naqobN , He perforated, pierced, bored, or made a hole through, or in, or into, anything: like vaqaba . (TA.) He made a hole through a wall. (S.) ― -b2- naqaba sur~apa Ald~aAb~api , aor. , He (a farrier) perforated the navel of the beast in order that a yellow fluid might issue forth. (S.) See manoqabN . ― -b3- naqaba AlEayona , aor. , inf. n. naqobN , He performed, upon the eye, what is called AlqadoHu in the language of the physicians; i. e., a remedial operation for the black fluid that arises in the eye: from the phrase next following: (IAth:) [but this is not a good explanation: the meaning is he performed upon the eye the operation of couching, for the cataract: so in many Arabic works, ancient and modern: (IbrD:) the couching-needle is called miqodaHN , and A_iborapu AlqadoHi , in the present day]. ― -b4- naqaba HaAfira Ald~aAb~api He (a farrier) pierced a hole in the hoof of the beast, in order to extract what had entered into it. (IAth.) ― -b5- naqabatohu nakobapN , (aor. , inf. n. naqobN , TA,) A misfortune, an evil accident, or a calamity befell him, (K,) and overcame him, or afflicted him; like nakabatohu . (TA.) [In the CK, for A^aSaAbatohu , is put AvAbth .] ― -b6- naqaba fiY AlA^aroDi , aor. , and ↓ Anqb and ↓ naq~b , He went, or went away, through the land, or country: (K:) [in the CK and some MS. copies of the K, we afterwards find naqiba fiY AlbilaAdi with kesr to the q , explained as signifying he proceeded, or journeyed, through the lands: ] ↓ Anqb he proceeded, or journeyed, through the country: (IAar:) nq~bwA fiY AlbilaAdi [Kur, l. 35,] they proceeded, or journeyed, through the lands, seeking for a place of refuge: (S:) or they traversed the lands, and journeyed through them, much, &c.: (Fr.:) or they went about and about, and searched, &c. (Zj.) fiY AlA=faAqi ↓ naq~abotu , in a verse of Imra-el-Keys, I journeyed through the tracts of the earth, and came and went. (TA.) ― -b7- naqiba AlbaEiyru , aor. , or naqiba Huf~u AlbEyri , (L, TA,) and ↓ Anqb , (L,) The camel walked barefooted, syn. HafiYa , (L, K,) until his feet became worn in holes: (TA:) or naqiba AlbEyr , (S, K,) and ↓ Anqb , (K,) the camel's feet became thin, [or were worn thin; which is also a signification of HafiYa ]. (S, K.) ― -b8- naqibato A^aqodaAmunaA Our feet became thin in the skin, and blistered, by reason of walking. (L.) ― -b9- naqaba Alxuf~a , aor. , He patched the boot; repaired it by patching. (K.) Also, He made the boot thin: he made [or wore ] holes in it. (Msb.) ― -b10- naqiba Alxuf~u , aor. , (inf. n. naqabN , TA,) The boot became lacerated, or worn through, in holes. (S, K, TA.) [And in like manner The sole of the foot of a camel or of a man: see below: and see an ex. voce A^aZal~u .] ― -b11- naqaba , aor. , inf. n. naqobN , He (a horse) put his feet together in his running ( fiY HuDorihi , [for which Golius and Freytag appear to have read fY xaSorihi ,] K,) not spreading his fore feet, his running being [ a kind of ] leaping. (TA.) -A2- naqaba Eani AlA^axoboAri , aor. , He scrutinized, investigated, searched into, examined into, or inquired into, the news; (K;) and, in like manner, anything else: (MF:) [as also ↓ nq~b : see the phrase nq~bwA fY AlblAd , explained above:] or he told, announced, or related, the news. (K.) ― -b2- A_in~iY lamo A^uw^omaro A^ano A^anoquba Eano quluwbi Aln~aAsi Verily I have not been commanded to scrutinize and reveal what is in the hearts of men. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b3- naqaba EalaY qawomihi , aor. , inf. n. niqaAbapN , He acted as the naqiyb over his people; was their nqyb : (S, K:) but of a man who was not nqyb , and has become so, you say naquba , with damm, aor. , inf. n. naqaAbapN , with fet-h, He became nqyb ; (Fr., S, K;) as also naqiba , aor. : (IKtt, K:) or nqAbp with kesr is a subst.; and with fet-h, an inf. n.; (S, K;) like wilaAyapN and walaAyapN : so says Sb. (S.) -A3- naqaba Alv~awoba , aor. , inf. n. naqobN , He made the piece of cloth into a nuqobap . (S.)

definition: [ A woman's face-veil;
sourceDefinition: [ A woman's face-veil; ] (S, K;) a veil that is upon [or covers ] the soft, or pliable, part of the nose; (AZ;) [ not extending higher: ] a woman's veil that extends as high as the circuit of the eye: (Msb:) it is of different modes: Fr says, When a woman lowers her nqAb to her eye, it [the action] is termed waSowaSapN ; and when she lowers it further, to [the lower part of] the circuit of the eye, it [the veil] is called nqAb ; and if it is on the extremity of the nose, it is [properly] called lifaAmN : (T:) the nqAb , with the Arabs, is that [ kind of veil ] from out of which appears the circuit of the eye: and the meaning of the saying in a trad. Aln~iqaAbu muHodavN is, that women's shewing the circuits of the eyes is an innovation; not that they used not to veil their faces: the [kind of] nqAb which they used reached close to the eye, and they showed one eye while the other was concealed; whereas the [kind of] nqAb , which only shows both the eyes [without their circuits] was called by them waSowaSapN [a mistake for waSowaASN ] and turoquEN : [in the original, wAlnqAb lA ybdwmnh Al~A AlEynAn wkAn Asmh Alx : but the w before kAn is erroneously introduced, and perverts the sense, which is otherwise plain, and agreeable with what is said before:] then they innovated the [veil] properly called] nqAb : (A'Obeyd:) pl. naqubN . (Msb.) -A2- niqaAbN and ↓ minaqabN A road through a rugged tract of ground: (K:) the former word used both as a sing and a pl. (TA.) -A3- niqaAbN (a strange form of epithet, MF,) (tropical:) A man of great knowledge; very knowing: (S, K:) or possessing a knowledge of things, or affairs: or, as also ↓ minEqabN , mentioned by I Ath and Z, a man possessing a knowledge of things, who scrutinizes or investigates them much; who is intelligent, and enters deeply into things. (TA.) -A4- nqaAbN The bello, Hence the proverb, faroxaAni fiY niqaAbK [ Two young birds in one belly ]: applied to two things that resemble one another, (K.) In like manner one says kaAnaA fiY nqAb waAHd [ They were in one belly ]; meaning they were like each other, (A.)

definition: Mind: syn. nafosN . (S, K,) You say fulaAnN mayomuwnu Alnqybpi Such a one is of a fortunate mind, (A'Obeyd, S,) when the person referred to is fortunate in his affairs, succeeding in what he seeks...
sourceDefinition: Mind: syn. nafosN . (S, K,) You say fulaAnN mayomuwnu Alnqybpi Such a one is of a fortunate mind, (A'Obeyd, S,) when the person referred to is fortunate in his affairs, succeeding in what he seeks after, or strives to accomplish: (ISk, S:) or when he is fortunate in his counsel, or advice: (Th, S:) or the phrase signifies such a one is fortunate in his actions, and in gaining what he seeks. (Msb, K, MS) and ; (Msb;) and nahisahu , aor. ; (Fr, K;) inf. n. nahosN (S, Msb, TA) and nuhosN ; (TA;) He (a man, S, Msb) took it (namely flesh or flesh-meat) with his fore teeth, (S, A, Msb, K,) to eat it, (Msb,) and plucked it off; (A, K;) as also ↓ Anthshu : (S:) and he ate it off from a bone ( taEar~aqahu ) with his fore teeth: (Lh, TA:) or he pulled it off with the central incisors, to eat it: (TA:) and he took it with the fore part of his mouth; as also ↓ Anthshu : (A:) or he took it with his mouth: (IAth, TA:) or he took it with his mouth to bite it and make a mark upon it without wounding it: (TA, art. nh$ :) and he (a dog, and any animal having a canine tooth,) bit it: or seized it, and then pulled it, or pulled it vehemently, or rent it with his teeth: but there is a difference of opinion respecting this verb in all its significations: some say that it is with the unpointed s ; and thus, only, it is mentioned by ISk, who says, I heard El-Kilábee say, of a dog and of a wolf and of a serpent, ↓ Anthshu and nahasahu ; (Msb;) [and J says, the nahos of the serpent is the same as its naho$ ; (S;) you say nahasatohu AlHay~apu in the sense of naha$atohu [ the serpent bit him ]: (Z, Sgh:) others say that the verbs are with s and $ throughout; and thus says IF on the authority of As: Az cites Lth as saying that naho$N , with the pointed $ , signifies taking, or reaching, from a distance, like the nh$ of the serpent; and nahosN , with the unpointed letter, the seizing upon flesh, or flesh-meat, and pulling it, or pulling it vehemently, or rending it with the teeth: Th says that the latter is with the extremities of the teeth; and the former, with the teeth [absolutely], and with [those that are termed] the A^aDoraAs : IKoot says, like Lth, that one says of the serpent ( AlHay~ap ), naha$atohu , with the pointed $ ; and of the dog and wolf and hyena, nahasahu , with the unpointed letter. (Msb.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yajibu , inf. n. wajobapN (Lh, K) and wajobN (Lh) It (a wall, or the like, Msb, or a house, or anything, Lh,) fell down. (Lh, K, Msb.) See wajobapN . ― -b2- wajaba , inf. n. wajobapN , It fell to the ground. (TA.) ― -b3- wajobapN does not signify a single act; but is an inf. n. in an absolute sense, unrestricted to the signification of a single act: ex. wajobapu Al$~amosi The falling of the sun, in setting. (TA.) ― -b4- faA_i*aA wajabato junuwbuhaA [Kur. xxii. 37,] is said to signify And when their sides fall down upon the ground: or and when their souls depart, and they fall down. (TA.) ― -b5- wajabati Al$~amosu , (S, K,) inf. n. wajobN and wujuwbN (K) and wajobapN (see above), The sun set. (S, K.) ― -b6- wajabati AlEayonu (tropical:) The eye was, or became, sunk in the head. (K.) ― -b7- wajaba , (S, K,) aor. yajibu , inf. n. wujuwbN and mawojibN , (TA,) He fell down and died: (S:) he died. (K.) ― -b8- Hudbeh Ibn-Khashram says, faqulotu lahu laA taboki Eayonuka A_in~ahu bikaf~aY~a maA laA qayotu A_i*o HaAna mawojibiY [ And I said to him, Let not thine eye weep; for by my own hands is occasioned what I experience, now that my death has come to pass ]. By mwjb he means mawotN . (TA.) ― -b9- [See also wajobapN , which seems to be a third inf. n. of the verb in this sense.] ― -b10- wajaba , (aor. yajibu , TA,) inf. n. wajiybN (Th, S,) and wajobN and wajabaAnN (K) and wujuwbN and wajobapN , (TA,) It (the heart) palpitated, beat, throbbed; (K;) was agitated, or in a state of commotion. (S.) ― -b11- wajabati AlA_ibilu , and ↓ wj~bt , The camels could scarcely arise from the places where they lay down. (TA.) ― -b12- waHuba , [aor. yawojubu ,] inf. n. wujuwbapN , He was cowardly, or pusillanimous. (S, K.) ― -b13- wajabahu Eanohu He drove him back, or turned him back, from it, (K,) when he had long kept to it. (Nawádir el-Aaráb.) -A2- wajaba and ↓ Awjb and ↓ wjb (tropical:) He (a man, TA,) ate once a day. (Th, K) See wajobapN . -A3- wajaba , aor. yajibu , inf. n. wujuwbN (S, K,) and jibapN , (K,) It (a thing) was, or became, necessitated, necessary, requisite, or unavoidable: it was binding, obligatory, incumbent, or due: syn. lazima ; (S, K, Msb;) [lit. accord. to some, it fell on a person: see 4;] and vabata , (Telweeh,) which means nearly the same as lazima . (TA.) ― -b2- For a fuller explanation, see its syn. Haq~a . [In the science of the fundamentals of religion, It necessarily was or existed; was a thing of which the nonexistence could not be mentally conceived: as is the essence of God. (Ibr. D.)] ― -b3- [ wajaba Ealayohi ka*aA , or A^ano yafaEala ka*aA , Such a thing, or the doing of such a thing, was binding, incumbent, or obligatory upon him; was unavoidable to him; lay on him; was his necessary, or indispensable duty: or was binding, incumbent, or obligatory upon him, by God's express appointment, so that he would be punished for neglecting it: and it was that which should be preferred and approved. See waAjibN .] ― -b4- See also another explanation, afterwards. ― -b5- wajaba AlbayoEu , aor. yajibu , inf. n. jibapN (Lh, S, Msb) and wujuwbN (Lh, Msb) The sale was, or became, binding, or obligatory; (Msb, TA;) ratified, fixed, settled, decided, or determined; (Msb;) completed, accomplished, or concluded; it had, or took, effect; it was extended, or performed; or it was, or became, effectual: (TA:) and wajabato yamiynuhu , i. q. bat~ato , q. v. (M, in art. bt .) ― -b6- It is said in a trad., A_i*aA kaAna AlbayoEu Eano xiyaArK faqado wajaba [ When the sale is optional, it is binding, or obligatory ]: i. e., when one says, after the contract, “ Take thy choice to reject the sale, or to make it effectual, ” and the person so addressed chooses to do the latter, the sale is binding, even if the two parties have not yet separated. (TA.) ― -b7- In like manner, wajaba AlHaq~u , inf. ns. as above, The right, due, or claim, was, or became, binding, or obligatory; or fixed, settled, decided, or determined. (Msb.) ― -b8- wjb Alwjb , inf. n. wjb : (TA: [unexplained; but following wajobN as signifying “ a bet, &c.: ” app. meaning The bet, wager, or stake, became due, or incumbent ]. ― -b9- [ wajaba Ealayoh It was, or became, necessitated, necessary, requisite, or unavoidable, for him to do, or suffer, such a thing; and hence, sometimes, it was, or became, binding, obligatory, or incumbent, on him. ] ― -b10- wajaba Ealayohi Alqawolu [ The saying or sentence became necessitated to take effect upon him; or it became requisite that the saying or sentence should take effect upon him. ] Jel, in xxxvi. 6, &c. ― -b11- [ wajaba lahu ka*aA Such a thing was, or became, due to him; as, for instance, a reward, or a punishment.] ― -b12- wajaba Ealayohi Alqatolu [ Slaughter was, or became, his due. ] (TA, in art. bqY , &c.)

definition: A daily allowance of food;
sourceDefinition: A daily allowance of food; or daily maintenance: syn. waZiyfapN : (K:) i. e., what a man is accustomed to allow himself [ each day ] as that which is necessary, and fixed: but the word in the A is wajobapN , q. v. (TA.) ― -b2- wajiybapN [ A term employed in the case of ] one's concluding a sale, and then taking it [ meaning what is sold to him ] by regular successive portions, one after another, (AA, S, K,) or, as some say, on the condition of his taking a portion of it every day, (TA,) until he has taken the whole of his wajiybap : (K:) [which hence appears to signify both the act above described and also what is due to one of a thing purchased and taken in this manner; but more probably the latter is the only meaning intended]. When a person has finished doing this, one says to him qadi A@sotawofayota wajiybataka [ Thou hast taken the whole of what was due to thee of the thing purchased and taken by thee in the manner above described ]. (S.)

definition: Slain: (S:) dying;
sourceDefinition: Slain: (S:) dying; or dead. (TA.) So in the following verse of Keys Ibn-ElKhateem: A^aTaAEato banuw EawofK A^amiyrFA nahaAhumu Eani Als~ilomi Hat~aY kaAna A^aw~ala waAjibi [ The sons of 'Owf obeyed a commander who forbade them to make peace until he was the first who was slain, or who died ]. (S, TA.) -A2- waAjibN [act. part. n. of wajaba ; Necessary; requisite; unavoidable: binding, incumbent, or obligatory. (IbrD.)] ― -b2- Accord. to [the Imám] Aboo-Haneefeh, waAjibN [in matters of religion] is not so strong a term as faroDN : [and so may be rendered incumbent, or obligatory; or that which is a necessary, or indispensable, duty; yet not so decisively or manifestly shown to be such as that which is termed frD :] or, accord. to Esh-Sháfi'ee, these two terms are syn., signifying [ binding, incumbent, or obligatory, by God's express appointment, as ] a thing for neglecting which one will be punished: and wAjb signifies that which should be preferred and approved; thus explained by ElKhattábee as occurring in the following trad.: gusolu AljumoEapi waAjibN EalaY kul~i muHotalimK The ablution prescribed to be performed on Friday is an act which every one who has experienced a nocturnal pollution should prefer and approve. (TA.) -A3- fiEolN waAjibN [ A verb expressing an event as a positive fact ] is such, for instance, as in the phrase bayonamaA A^anaA ka*aA A_i*o jaA='a zayodN [while I was thus, or in [this state, lo, or behold, Zeyd came]. (S, L, art. A* .)

definition: A covenant, compact, or contract: (S, K:) a dial.
sourceDefinition: A covenant, compact, or contract: (S, K:) a dial. form of A_iSorN ; like as they said A_irovN and wirovN , and A_isaAdapN and wisaAdapN . (S.) ― -b2- Also, (S, A, K,) and ↓ waSar~apN (Lth, A, K) and ↓ waSiyrapN (K) and ↓ A^awoSarN , (Lth, TS, L,) A written statement of a purchase or sale, transfer, bargain, or contract: (S, A, K, TA:) the first is from A_iSorN , and is generally used in this sense: pl. of the first, A^awoSaArN ; and of the second, waSar~aAtN : Lth says, that the second is an arabicized word; and others say, that the first and second are Persian words, arabicized. (TA.) One says, A^aqoTaEahu AlA^aroDa wakataba lahu AlwiSora , and ↓ AlwaSar~apa , [ He made him a grant of the land to be held in fee, and wrote for him the statement of the transfer. ] (A.) (S.)

definition: , [coll. gen. n., The sapphire, of whatever variety: the ruby, oriental ruby, or red sapphire, also called yAqwtN A^aHomaru ; of which there are several varieties, whereof one is the carbuncle; also...
sourceDefinition: , [coll. gen. n., The sapphire, of whatever variety: the ruby, oriental ruby, or red sapphire, also called yAqwtN A^aHomaru ; of which there are several varieties, whereof one is the carbuncle; also called yAqwtN jamoriY~N : the sapphire, commonly so called, or blue sapphire, also called yAqwtN A^azoraqu : and the topaz, oriental topaz, or yellow sapphire, also called yAqwtN A^aSofaru : the jacinth, or hyacinth, accord. to Golius, who observes, as on the authority of the Teyfáshee, that by this name are called various gems of the East; four species thereof being enumerated; the red, the yellow, or gold-coloured, the blue, or azure, and the white: that the sapphire and the chrysolite are also thus called: but that, by the word used absolutely, the red jacinth, or hyacinth, commonly called the ruby, is meant: which last remark is agreeable with modern usage:] a well known gem; (K;) of which there are many varieties, (TA,) the most excellent whereof is that called AlyAqwtu AlA^aHomaru Alr~um~aAniY~u , (K,) also called AlbahoramaAniY~u ; [the finest kind of ruby or carbuncle; ] said to be brought from Sarandeeb [or Ceylon]: it has the property of exhilarating, and of conjoining [separated friends]; (TA;) and is profitable for disturbance of the mind (occasioned by the black bile, TA) and palpitation, and weakness of the heart and stomach, if drunk; [being app. reduced to powder for that purpose, as is done with some other gems in the East;] and for congealment of the blood, if hung [upon the person]: (K:) it is a Persian word, (S,) arabicized: (S, K:) of the measure faAEuwlN : n. un. with p ; and pl. yawAqiytu . (S.)
